Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment) moved the second reading, of and concurrence in amendments made by the Senate to Bill No. 32, respecting the disposal of the canteen funds.
He said:	Perhaps a word of explanation
might be in order. The House will remember that the bill as originally presented to the House of Commons received more than ordinary attention. It provides for the disposal of canteen funds amounting to about $21550,000 more or less, and the Senate has amended it in one important respect. There are other amendments of minor importance but the one to which I refer is the amendment which removes from the bill the cause or subsection providing that an amount of $100,000 shall be placed in the hands of the central board of trustees for the maintenance in Ottawa of a central adjustment bureau. The Senate has found it advisable to remove that feature from the bill. If I read the subsection perhaps hon. members will more readily understand the nature of the change:
That the sum of $100,000 shall be allotted and paid to the central board of trustees to be expended by such board from time to time in such amounts and in such manner as i-t may be deemed best for the maintenance and assistance of an adjustment service and bureau at Ottawa for the benefit of ex-members of the forces and their dependents.
This has been deleted. The Senate has also struck out the provision contained in section 3 for the appointment by the Governor in Council of a central board of trustees. If therefore we accept the amendments of the Senate this amount of $100,000 will not be handed over to anyone except to the parties mentioned for the general distribution, that is to say, the provincial governments. In this connection I have received a communication dated June 10, on behalf of a number of soldier organizations in Canada. Perhaps I had better read it:
Canteen Funds

Dear Sir,-At a meeting of the representatives of the Dominion chartered associations enumerated below held at the Trusts Building, Ottawa, on Monday, June 8, the following resolution was passed unanimously:
" That the time has arrived when no further grants be made by the government from canteen or public funds to any veterans' association for the purpose of establishing and maintaining a service or adjustment veterans' bureau in Ottawa."
That communication is signed by the actingsecretary, Mr. Keeling, who states that the following representatives were present:	One
frofil the Canadian Legion, one from the Army and Navy Veterans, one from the Grand Army of United Veterans, one from the Amputations Association, one from the Tuberculous Veterans' Association. These different bodies were represented at that meeting and expressed the view that no canteen funds should be appropriated for the purpose of maintaining an adjustment bureau, at least so far as they were concerned. The only large association that does not appear to have been represented at the meeting is the Great War Veterans' Association. I have not read the evidence given before the Senate committee, but I am informed that the secretary-treasurer of the Great War Veterans' Association in his testimony stated that the association did not desire to administer the adjustment bureau. It would appear therefore that the veterans generally are more or less hostile to the adjustment bureau. This clause I introduced on the suggestion of the royal commission. In view of these circumstances, I do not think it would be in order to ask the House to pray the Senate to desist from their amendment.
There is another amendment by the Senate which perhaps is a little more embarrassing. A sum of five thousand pounds was handed to His Excellency the Governor General from the United Services Fund of England for distribution amongst ex-imperial soldiers in Canada. I understand the money has been placed by His Excellency in the hands of the Receiver-General, with an intimation to the government that appropriate action would be taken for its distribution. The Senate has removed this feature from the bill. No reason is given for their action, except that the distribution was to have been made by the Central Board of Trustees. If the bill passes in its amended form there will be no provision at all for the distribution of this five thousand pound fund, except in so far as the government may think proper to proceed after prorogation. I cannot say at present what action we will take with respect to it. I may say, however, that I would be inclined to hand over the five thousand pounds to the Canadian Red Cross Society for distribution.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. S. BELAND (Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment):
speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there is a small amendment made to clause 1 which I do not consider of any importance. It is the removal of the words, " or attributable to," which we inserted in this House. Clause 3 has been struck out. It provided for an extension of five years for the payment of pensions to dependents of pensioners in classes one to five. I shall have a word to say about this amendment a little later on. The Senate has also amended section 13 of the act, providing that applications for pensions may be received within seven years after the date of discharge. This is quite agreeable to me and, I think, should be to the House.
Will this have the effect of increasing the number of pensioners, and therefore the charges on the revenues of the *country?

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext: It will to a certain degree.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
My hon. friend's point is
perhaps well taken. But the Pension Act may be said to be different from any other act, because tha payment of pensions is really in charge of a body which has judicial functions beyond the power of parliament. Another amendment which has been made has relation to marriage after the appearance of disability. This question of the payment of pension to widows whose marriage to the returned man took place after the appearance of disability has engaged the attention of parliament more or less since 1919, and there has been a wide difference of opinion with respect to it, both in the parliamentary committee and on the floor of the House. It is a very important clause. I remember when we discussed it in the first instance the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Boys) said that the clause was certainly not clear. It is very involved indeed. In view of the number of amendments to the Pension Act this vear, however, that are really favourable to the returned men generally I do not thing we should ask that the Senate desist from this amendment. Section 10 of the bill which is deleted by the Senate amendments, provides
for the payment of pension to widowed mothers who become dependent after the death of the son. I may say that the office of the minister is deluged with correspondence from all over the country, much of it consisting of complaints with regard to the provisions of the act, or the action of the Board of Pension Commissioners, but I do not think I have received a single complaint from widowed mothers who had become dependent and who had been awarded a pension below the maximum. I believe they have received pensions commensurate with their need, and I do not think we should insist that this clause remain in the bill. Another amendment made by the Senate is of a more serious character. It is to section 16 and has relation to appeals to the Federal Appeal Board. The Board of Pension Commissioners have decided in some cases that pensions could not be awarded where the disability was the result of misconduct. In every case where such a decision was brought to my attention and the soldier thought he had not been fairly dealt with, I advised an appeal, and in some cases where appeal was taken the appeal board sustained it, that is, declared that the disability was attributable to military service. The Board of Pension Commissioners, however, have taken the ground that from a decision on their part that a disability was the result of misconduct there is no appeal; that such a matter is beyond the jurisdiction of the Federal Appeal Board, and the Justice department have upheld that view. But I do not think it is fair that a man whose application is turned down by the Board of Pension Commissioners because his disability is alleged to be the result of misconduct should have no appeal. We had provided in the bill as follows:
"Upon the evidence and record upon which the Board of Pension Commissioners gave their decision an appeal shall lie in respect of any refusal of pension by the Board of Pension Commissioners on the ground that the injury or disease or aggravation thereof resulting in disability or death was not attributable to or was not incurred during military service or was the result of misconduct."
These last six words, which are added to the former clause, have now been deleted by the Senate, so that where the Board of Pension Commissioners decide that a man's disability is the result of misconduct he is precluded from appeal. In my opinion, where a man is turned down on that ground the decision means that his disability is not attributable to military service, but if the decision were simply that his disability was not attributable to war service, he would 'have an appeal under the act. According to the Justice department he has

no appeal where the ground for the rejection of the application is that the disability was the result of misconduct. I think, therefore, that we should a& the Senate not to insist on that amendment. There are only twelve cases involved, I understand, but even twelve cases should not be wrongly dealt with. It does not mean that these men will receive pension or will not; it simply means that when the board decides that the disability is the result of misconduct, if the soldier holds that the disability is not the result of misconduct but is attributable to service, he should have the privilege of appealing to the Federal Appeal Board.

I think the hon. member for Kingston and myself disagree with the minister vqry seriously there, because cases arise-and there are now cases in appeal- where there was no manifestation of the disease during military service, and the whole case turns on the question of attributability.
I thought, and I still think it would be wise to retaiu these words.

speakerposition: Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment; Minister presiding over the Department of Health
speechtext:
I have no objection to asking the Senate to leave in those words. I do not think there would be very much objection to that. But I would point out that even if the disease manifests itself long after discharge, a decision must be given as to 
whether it was incurred during military service or not, and in my humble opinion the words my hon. friend suggests have a narrower interpretation than the phrase " incurred during military service." But, at all events, that is a matter that can be adjusted in the motion.
The Senate has agreed with very important clauses that we have passed at this session. For instance, the House has made the bonus a permanent part of the pension this session; that clause has been left intact by the Senate. That is clause 13. Another amendment dealing with venereal disease contracted prior to enlistment which was passed by the House has also been left intact. Another clause which deals with tubercular pensioners and the payment of pensions to them after discharge from, hospital has also been respected in its entirety by the Senate. There was also a new provision that an allowance for wear and tear for clothing should be made in amputation cases; that has also been left in its entirety; also the payment of pensions to parents who-are in dependent circumstances, when the son still living is by reason of certain circumstances unable to provide for their support has been left intact.
The House will remember that we made an important amendment this year which provided for no cancellation of pension in the case of an alleged prostitute until the opportunity had been offered to the woman to present her defence. That also has been maintained. I move:

Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Justice) moved the second reading of Bill No. 209, to amend the Canada Temperance Act.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) :
speechtext: I would like to say a word1 in opposition to the principle of this bill. I am afraid that I am rather in a minority in this House on the question, but nevertheless with the feeling that I am right, I am going to put before the House the proposition which I think ought to govern in this case. This bill, or a similar bill, has been before the House for the last three or four years. It seeks to give the attorney general of the province where it is going to be put into effect the right to declare prohibition by order in council. Up to the present every province which has prohibition in force has had first to obtain from this parliament the right to hold a plebiscite, and when the plebiscite was granted and a vote was taken in the province upon it, they had the right to put prohibition into effect. But under the present legislation no plebiscite will be necessary. The parliament of Canada gives to the province the right to say that, upon an order in council being passed by the province without any plebiscite, prohibition will go into effect, and furthermore it also gives the province the right to revoke this prohibition and put the province in the same place as it was before. That means that if at any time they feel they do not want prohibition in any province, that province need not come to parliament, but can declare that ipso facto prohibition is revoked and is no longer in effect. So that we the parliament of Canada delegate to the provinces the right to do something which they never had before. The point I am trying to urge on the House is that there should be a plebiscite in the provinces which are seeking to obtain prohibition before they can put it into effect. The other provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta, Nova Scotia, and others, that have had prohibition, obtained it only after a plebiscite was taken. The province of British Columbia, which I understand is the principal one interested in this particular act, wishes to put this law into effect without going through the procedure which the other provinces were obliged to go through, and for that reason I object to the bill.

A poor reason.
Mr. JACOBS. It is the best I have.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think my hon. friend is under a misapprehension when he states that this will place all the power in the hands of one man. That was the objection [DOT] to the bill two years ago, because this matter
Canada Temperance Act

When I say one man, I
mean the lieutenant governor in council. I was thinking of the attorney general.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I am glad my hon.
friend says it is not one man, but the government of the province. Two years ago, when this bill passed the House of Commons, an exception was made in the bill permitting export warehouses to import liquor, but they had to obtain leave from the attorney general of the province. This provision was strongly objected to in this House, and my hon. friends who were opposed to the bill pointed out that it was giving a tremendous power to one man. The government then moved to strike out this exception in favour of the export houses altogether, and the objection in regard to giving the power to the attorney general was eliminated. The bill passed this House and was amended in the Senate in such a way that it was not acceptable to this Chamber. All the provinces at the present time, except British Columbia and Quebec, have held a plebiscite and have placed themselves under Part IV of the Canada Temperance Act; that is to say complete prohibition. Three of those provinces, Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, have modified that situation since by adopting the system of government sale of liquor. British Columbia and Quebec never held a plebiscite under Part IV of the Canada Temperance Act, but both held plebiscites for the purpose of having government control of liquor. A plebiscite was held in British Columbia and the people of the province voted that liquor should be sold in British Columbia by the government or by a board or commission appointed by the government. The purpose of this bill is that in those provinces Where government control of liquor is in force, where they have not placed themselves under Part IV of the Canada Temperance Act, when the lieutenant governor of the province by order in council asks the Governor in Council of Canada to apply in that province prohibition of the importation of all liquors except by the government, or the commission intrusted by the government the power of selling liquor, with certain exceptions provided in the bill, the Governor in Council Shall issue a proclamation giving effect to the will of the province manifested by its government that there should be no more importation of liquor.
]Mr. Lapointe.]
This legislation has been requested very urgently by the government of British Columbia. This House accepted it two years ago, and by moving the second reading of this bill and submitting it to the House, I am only conforming to the principle which seems to have been adopted in this country, that the will of the provinces in this matter should prevail. If British Columbia wants prohibition of importations except through the government, I think we should enact legislation to put that situation into effect?

Mr. Speaker, I should like to lend what support I can to the passage of this bill. The suggestion made by the hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) that it is putting too much power into the hands of one man, has been met already by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) stating that it is not one man, it is the government of the province. The government of the province is responsible to the people of British Columbia, and they will know how to deal with any attempt to hold up the liquor interests. The liquor interests, as we know them in British Columbia, are abundantly able to take care of themselves. There is no danger of their being held up in any sense of the term. As regards the remarks of an hon. member opposite in reference to a plebescite, we do not want any more plebescites in British Columbia. We have taken three plebescites on this question already and now we want some action. We have fully expressed in British Columbia what we want. The principal advantage of this bill, to my mind, is in doing away with the export houses. Export houses were done away with in Saskatchewan and Alberta in 1922, and I do not know of any complaints of any unjustices or misfortunes that have happened to those provinces as a consequence. The system does harm in British Columbia in many ways, but I will name three of them. First, there is a heavy loss of revenue to the Dominion government because they evade the excise. Gf course the liquor is ostensibly exported to go to Mexico -that is the usual clearing paper-and then it is taken down to 'Frisco or Washington and sold there. In this case the duty will be paid. It has become a regular standard trade to bootleg the liquor back into British Columbia. It is taken a few miles from the harbour in a boat apparently on its way to Mexico. It is brought back after dark and put into the hands of a bootlegger-not the casual drink peddler you meet on the street corner, but established houses-and then it is sold to the public at a price far below that at which the government can sell it because they have not paid the excise. Very often they omit the formality

of taking it down the Sound. They take it in a truck from one place in the city to another. If some prohibition officer interferes, the truck breaks down and the stuff is taken back whence it came. If they are pushed to it, they will get a boat next day and take it out.
Is the hon. member describing conditions as they exist to-day in British Columbia?

Yes. It is also bringing the whole law into contempt in British Columbia. It- has got to be now quite a respectable thing to be a bootlegger; you rank between a deacon of the church, and a bishop. I know of people who move in good society who are not ashamed to say that they have made, are making and will continue to make, money in that way. This leads to contempt of the law in other respects also. We are getting familiarized with breaking the law and this is spreading in other lines. This is a paper I received to-day, the Vancouver Daily Province, which says in big headlines:
Baker and Sowash will hang September 4.
What are they to hang for? For the murder of two men that were hi-jacked. "Hijacking" is another branch of this beautiful system. When this man takes out booze going to Mexico or the United States, he is doing so illegally and, therefore, he more or less ceases to be under the protection of the law. Some man comes along with a faster boat, and by means of coercion, possibly with a shotgun, he takes the liquor away from the other man. The man who has been robbed of his liquor cannot squeal because he is outside the pale of the law. Thus we have this other occupation known as hi-jacking. These two men who are going to hang on September 4 hi-jacked two men on a boat. They murdered them. Four men were concerned in this. They have got two and the other two they will get yet. Thus, six lives are to be snuffed out as a result of an every day occurrence of this trade. This hi-jacking is going on, not only on the high seas, but on the roads where they are transporting the liquor by means of motor trucks. To have your liquor hi-jacked is a common occurrence, and it is recognized as one of the expenses of the business.
Does the hon. member believe, if this legislation goes into force, all the hi-jacking is going to be done away with?
Ninety per cent of it.

What about the United
States? They have a prohibition law in force there and conditions are just about the same as he has depicted them in British Columbia.

The hon. member is talking
from the other side of the line, so to speak. I am not responsible for conditions in the United States. They are doing their utmost to enforce the law there, and they are very much handicapped by the illicit trade that is going on from British Columbia. That brings me to another phase of the argument why we should pass this bill. It is an important one in these days of international relationships. This traffic is highly productive of friction between us and the United States. We are further away here from the border and we do not see these things. But in British Columbia, we see it going on all the time, and it is very much calculated to cause ill-will between the United States and us. A boat called the Quadra was seized the other day on the California coast from British Columbia with a large cargo running into hundreds of thousands of dollars' worth. The case came into court. The question arose whether this boat was really within an hour's run-I think that is the limit prescribed-from their coast when it was seized or not. It was held by those defending the Quadra's crew and captain that the court unjustly ruled against allowing any evidence to show where this boat was at the time. Naturally it was commented on very strongly and harshly in our local papers. International friction was engendered at once. It is alleged that these British Columbia men, some twenty in number, who are in jail now awaiting trial, had not a fair chance, because the judge took the opposite view in the American court. Incidents like that are occurring all the time, and sooner or later they are going to lead to an international question that is quite unnecessary and highly to be avoided. It says somewhere: A man who would have friends must show himself friendly. A man who would have good neighbours must be neighbourly himself. We are not acting as a good neighbour towards the United States when we encourage this illicit traffic.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill) is expecting altogether too much in the way of reform as a result of this legislation. He speaks of the evils of the export houses. He seems to overlook the fact that those export houses exist only at the will of the government of British Columbia, and in fact, at the will of the Attorney General of British Columbia. They all have to come to him for licenses, and if he did not wish them to exist and operate, they would not be there at all. They cannot operate with
Canada Temperance Act

a license from the Attorney General of British Columbia.

It is not a license, it is
only his consent to a license issued by the Dominion, if my hon. friend will excuse my correcting his law.

That may be a
distinction without a difference.
No.

There is not an
export house that is operating in British Columbia to-day that does not have to have the approval of the Attorney General of British Columbia, and in many cases licenses were issued to those export houses situated in the interior of British Columbia where there was no possibility of their doing a legitimate export business. If they had been down at the coast where goods could have been exported to foreign countries, the matter would have been different. It was a standing joke in British Columbia that export houses were applying for licenses so that they might make illegitimate exports to the United States which was the only place where they could run their goods. These licenses were issued wilfully with the approval of the Attorney General of British Columbia, and it is idle for hon. members to pretend that in asking for this legislation he wants to prevent illegalities or bootlegging. It is only a sham fight that is being put up by British Columbia against bootlegging; it is one of their chief sources of revenue. I see no reason why this question should be dealt with in British Columbia on any basis different from that adopted in other provinces. When the people of other provinces desire a change in their liquor law they express that desire at the polls; but this question has not been voted upon in British Columbia. That is the principal objection to the bill; it is wrong in principle. This is a pointed case of establishing government by order in council, and that I should think would be the last thing that this government would want to encourage. There is no necessity for the bill. It is an encroachment on private rights and until we have some expression from the people of British Columbia that they want such legislation, I submit it should not be enacted.

It is said that there has been no plebiscite in British Columbia on this question, but that is not correct. There was a plebiscite and it carried by the largest majority ever secured on any question voted upon by the people of that province. The people gave the government

control over the liquor question and unless this legislation is passed that government will not have that control. The provincial government wants this legislation enacted and the people want it.
Does the hon. member suggest that the government of British Columbia has not now as complete control over the operations of the export liquor houses as it will have after this bill becomes law?

Absolutely no. As I say, both the government and the prohibition people as well as those who have the interests of the province at heart have demanded this legislation in order to put a stop to the traffic in liquor which is going on between the province and the United States. This traffic is creating a hard feeling between the United States and the people of British Columbia, and indeed, of Canada as a whole, and it is felt that this government is responsible for it. If this legislation is carried it will end the traffic, and as the people of the province are asking for it I see no reason why it should not be adopted.

speechtext: I believe my hon. friend is right, that they do not issue licenses except with the approval of the attorney general However, it is considered wise to have this provision.

As for the picture painted
by my hon. friend (Mr. McBride), the government can absolutely control the situation to-day; they are responsible for the conditions that exist. Why should we enable the government of British Columbia to bring certain legislation into effect, to cancel it, to bring it back into force again, and to switch it around any way they like, when they already have the situation absolutely in their control if they desire to take advantage of the power they now have.

The hon. member is working both ends against the middle. It is true that the attorney general of the province must give his consent before the license is issued, but that consent has reference only to the surrounding conditions, because he has not the power of absolute refusal. Anyone who wants a license gets it from this government and all that the attorney general of the province has to do with it is to exercise an advisory supervision, so to speak, over the circumstances in which the license shall apply. He may say that this is the wrong place, or that the circumstances are undesirable, and so on but he cannot positively withhold the license, inasmuch as it is this government that issues it. As regards the objection that the attorney general can already do what it is proposed to enable him to do, the hon. member (Mr. Clark) stated a few minutes ago that he did not want to see so much power put into the hands of that officer. Apparently he has not much confidence in the attorney general of the province, and when the Minister of Justice pointed out that it was not the attorney general but the government of the province that had the say, the hon. member transferred his distrust to the government. He suspects that proper use will not be made of the power which is being
enacted, because, he says, this has been the case in the past. Now, what is the objection to this legislation, which will absolutely prohibit by Dominion law the importation of liquor for export? It would appear to me that it is not going to do any harm if everything the hon. member has said is correct.

That is just where my hon. friend is mistaken. This is order in council legislation, and not until the government passes an order in council does it come into effect. To-day the Attorney General of British Columbia can positively stop the issuance of a license to any government export house in the province. The Minister of Customs and Excise (Mr. Bureau) has so stated in this House. All he has to do now is to withhold his consent and the license will not issue. The only additional power given by this legislation is to prohibit private individuals importing liquor.

Mr. Chairman, I quite agree with What t'he hon. member for Burrard (Mr. Clark) has stated. When the Attorney General of British Columbia refuses to give his consent to the issuing of a license, it practically puts an end to the efforts of any person to get a license here in Ottawa, and so far as I know the Customs and Excise department have never issued a license where the attorney general of the province has refused to give his consent either through whim or otherwise. No, those are hot
drawbacks.

It just shows how senseless this is, because sometimes a bald-headed man has as much inside his head as many others have outside. But I am afraid that when I refer to bald heads in this House I am treading on dangerous ground. That disposes of the question raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Neill). Let us assume that this measure will be passed-and I am inclined to think that it will be-the government of British Columbia need never put it into force at all; it simply transfers from the federal authority to the provincial authority all federal rights. That, it seems to me, is giving that province more power than the other provinces, because the latter had to proceed by way of plebiscite. Hon. gentlemen have stated that three or four plebiscites were taken in British Columbia. But those plebiscites were only on the question of government control, and the Minister

of Justice admits it. The Quebec legislature has passed an act declaring that no one except the provincial government can traffic in liquor. I believe in putting all the provinces on the same plane. Every province that wishes to carry on business in this particular way should take a plebiscite before it goes into the business. The only result of increasing the license fee to ten thousand

dollars was the amalgamation of a large number of export warehouses into bigger and more powerful business enterprise. Has the Minister of Justice any assurance from the government of British Columbia that upon the adoption of this legislation it will be immediately put into force by the province?

speechtext: The government of British Columbia have been so insistent in asking for this legislation that the advisability of asking them whether they were going to take advantage of it never entered my mind. speechtext: Ontario is under part four of the Canada Temperance Act. She had a plebiscite and a proclamation was issued accordingly.

Canada Temperance Act

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is nothing extraordinary about it. Those provinces which have been desirous of adopting Part IV of the act have done so. There are two provinces which have not adopted Part IV, but both of them have government control of liquor. Plebiscites have been held in both those provinces as a result of which the people asked for that government control. Is there anything extraordinary in the proposal that when any one of these provinces asks that importation of liquor be prohibited otherwise than by or through the government, subject to certain exceptions, the will of the province shall be ratified and agreed to by the Governor in Council?

I think there is. Ontario ran wild with these export houses until they took action to deal with the matter. I was in the legislature and I know there were dozens of them until the province put a stop to it. I think British Columbia should do the same.
Why is a special exception made in favour of British Columbia with respect to plebiscite? Why should they not have a plebscite as the other provinces have had?

Not on this question.

The government of British Columbia represent the people of that province, and the leader of that government was down here and asking for this legislation. They seemed to think that unless this legislation passed they could not control liquor there as they would wish to. Why should we quibble over these things when the government which represents British Columbia ask for this legislation?
It is not a question of quibbling; it is a question of observing the rights of the people of British Columbia.
The bootleggers.

Not the bootleggers; I do not thank the hon. member for that remark. I am just as anxious as he is to see the liquor business of British Columbia or of Canada generally put on a proper and decent basis if it can be done. But in my opinion the application for this legislation is not bona fide; is not for that purpose; is designed simply to put a club in the hands of the Attorney General of British Columbia to be used by him politically and for no
other reason. When the hon. members for Comox-Albemi and Cariboo say that a plebiscite on this question has been held, they do not speak by the book; they are mistaken. There was a plebiscite on the question whether there should be government sale of liquor, prohibition or whether we should continue in the old way of sale in public bars, and the plebiscite went in favour of sale by the government. But the vote taken at that time and the legislation enacted thereunder in no way dealt with the question of private importation; that question has never been submitted to the electors of British Columbia. deepening of channels and the dredging of these rivers be covered by the .covenant and agreement by Which the minister said they were bound?

You have to keep them to a certain depth. In those waters, of course, there is continual silting and that kind of thing. Part of the canal is eight feet four inches, and part of it is six feet. that the authority rested with the federal government, and so the federal government is responsible.

What is the policy of
the department in connection with building small wharves on the lakes on the Trent canal? For a number of years it was the policy of the department to construct small wharves for the accommodation of boats calling at the different little summer resorts. While possibly a great deal of criticism may be made of expenditures in connection with the Trent canal, yet I fear that to-day very few of us realize what value the Trent canal is to Canada. It is a great inducement to the tourist traffic. It gives them travelling facilities up and down the canal. While there are parts of it that never should have been built, yet I feel that the money spent in constructing the connecting links between the chains of lakes was money well spent and those channels should be kept in proper shape. In this way the tourist traffic is given the encouragement it deserves, and few of us realize the value to Canada today of the tourist traffic. It would be wisdom on the part of the government to see that small wharves are constructed at an expenditure of from $2,000 to $4,000 or $5,000, to accommodate small boats. Many tourists like to have their mail come to them by boat at the small resorts.

It would be hard to announce a policy as to small wharves. It might mean many dozens of small wharves. At the entrances to locks, of course, there is always accommodation and I think the chief places have their locks. I would not like to say that the government was ready to construct a wharf at every place where a few people congregated for the summer. We have many applications, but as a general rule we do not go into the dockbuilding business very extensively along the Trent system. Hon. members who have never been through the Trent system, ought to go through it before they criticize it very much. More money is coming to Canada every year through the tourist traffic than, perhaps, people are aware of, and this is one of the most beautiful spots in the Dominion or, in fact, the continent of America. The tourist traffic through it is growing every year and the money they expend there cannot be counted in small figures. In addition to that the federal government collected last year $152,000 in income, not from the docks, but from waterpowers that have been leased along the Trent.

What was the total
amount spent by the Dominion government?
307i

The minister stated that he did not think it was wise for the department to begin the construction of wharves at every place where requests were made for them. I do not think there is any danger that they will get into a condition of that kind and build structures wherever they are requested. But there are places with anywhere from seventy-five to one hundred and fifty summer cottages where some accommodation is badly needed. The boats to-day run their bow up on the shore and in windy weather they are obliged to go by with the mail or have another boat come out and meet them. It is important that we should cater to the tourist traffic in the Highlands of Ontario. We have something to sell in that regard which is not equalled anywhere else in Canada, and where public highways lead up to resorts of this kind of any considerable size it would be well for the government to provide some small accommodation to enable the boats to land.

Will it be necessary for these contracts to run on forever? We spent on this canal up to the end of the fiscal year 1925 the sum of $23,443,742, and these expenditures have been going on since 1882. In view of our present financial standing some effort should be made to stop the leak. I would ask the minister for some information regarding these contracts.

My hon. friend knows that these are old agreements outstanding between the Dominion and the provincial government, and we might just as well attempt to remove the dams that protect the people living on any part of the Ottawa river as allow these dams to become, not dilapidated but in any degree unsafe. My hon. friend will understand the situation only as a result of a trip through that part of the country. He talks about "stopping the leak," but we are forgetting, or we have not yet learned, the benefit of the tourist traffic to the country. We have one of the most beautiful countries in the world. Those of us who have been in Switzerland know perfectly well that that countiy has nothing on Canada for scenic beauty; yet we shrink at any expenditure to develop the traffic. There are places in Canada where not much grain is produced and one of the sources of revenue is just this traffic. The people in this part of the country depend almost entirely on the business that

Supply-Railways and Canals
results from the visit of tourists, and for that reason this expenditure can more readily be justified -perhaps than others. We cannot afford to abandon the Trent canal with all its dams and other protective works. If we failed to keep them in a constant state of repair there would be a danger of the surrounding country being flooded, and we are not allowed to neglect them under the agreement we have with the province. If we abandoned this work it would cost us millions of dollars, to say nothing of the wanton destruction to property.

Is it contemplated carrying
the canal through to Georgian bay?

It is all through except for the completion of the portion of work on the Severn river which is not yet done. Small marine railways are being used to take the fifteen-ton boats from one point to another of navigation, and the completion of the remaining portion of work is all that is necessary to have the waterway capable of carrying hundreds of thousands of tourists from Georgian bay clear to lake Ontario.
Does Switzerland build canals to develop the tourist traffic there?

She does everything of
that kind. She spends millions of dollars developing the scenery and as a consequence cities like Geneva are crowded the year round with tourists. In Germany, instead of building branch railways to places that can be reached otherwise, small waterways are built along which industries are started. Germany is dotted with scenes of this sort. I have been on canals there where they pumped the water from one part into another, and I can assure the committee that the Trent canal is a prince to most of them.

For the information of those who criticize the expenditures to develop our natural scenery, I may say that during the tourist season last summer for some two and a half months two little villages in my constituency, each with a branch bank and with a population, one of 800 and the other of 900, took in respectively $44,000 and $27,000 of American money. That gives a slight idea of the value of the tourist traffic to that part of the country.

Is the tourist traffic
fairly steady, or does it fluctuate? I notice looking back over the record of the work done that the expenditure has always increased around election time and I was wondering whether there was any particular influx of tourists on such occasions.
There might be.

Board of Railway Commissioners for Canada: maintenance and operation of, $239,339.
Does the government propose to increase the membership of the commission?

There is nothing in the
estimates for the purpose, anrt m wVuiu require legislation to either increase or diminish the board. The board was constituted along certain lines, and I had the honour some years ago of introducing legislation to enlarge it. although I think the board is, if anything, too unwieldy already, that does not at all shut out consideration of the suggestion that there might be some reorganization of the board in the future.

I am not particularly anxious to have the board enlarged, but I should like to see it more representative of the different sections of the Dominion. Western Canada has only one representative on the board, and I think we contribute the major portion of the net earnings of the Canadian Pacific. With the passage of the railway freight rates legislation within the past few days, the protection which the Crowsnest pass agreement gave us on every commodity except grain and flour has been removed, and we are now left altogether -if I may be pardoned for using the expression -at the mercy of the Board of Railway Commissioners. Does the minister think we are fairly represented on that board? If not, are we likely to receive justice from the board? This is a very important matter to western Canada, and there is a strong feeling in the west that we should have greater representation on the board-one member out of six is altogether inadequate.

When the board was first established the object was to get the best men to undertake the work, no matter where they came from, because, considering the diversity of interests throughout the Dominion, the board has a very difficult task to perform. As in any other business the man who will do the best is the man who ought to be on the board. If I were hiring a man to do my business I would not care where he came from so long as he did his work satisfactorily. The suggestion of having a man from the west is worthy of consideration, although I would not admit that any other man would not give the west justice. But the western man might understand the psychology of the western people at least a little better than a man from some other part of the country.

I agree with the minister that this board is too large and will have to be reorganized, and the quickest way to reorganize it is to consolidate the two railways. If that is done you will not have all this competition for traffic between two companies, to say nothing of outside companies, and there will not be one quarter of the work that is now imposed on the railway commission. You do not improve matters by increasing the number of members of the commission; in fact you only make things worse. But when you simplify the railway system you can reduce the personnel and simplify the operations of the board of railway commissioners, as well as effect an economy of 5100,000,000 a year-the best authorities say $150,000,000. This is the only way parliament can get control of railway rates; we will save money, have a better system and get a better service.

The best member of the
board now is a western man. I have heard it remarked that he spends most of his time writing dissenting judgments.

I see he gave one the
other day in which he was in accord with the rest of the board.

Perhaps the exception proves the rule. I think there is a great deal of misapprehension with regard to the work of the Board of Railway Commissioners. We often hear it stated that the matter of making railway rates should be left entirely to the board. I doubt very much whether the board has ever made a rate; they have only put their stamp of approval upon rates that are made by the railway companies. Whenever there is any rate making, it is by the railway companies themselves, and if no one objects after the rates are posted up in the office of the rail-

way commission, they are approved of by the board. I would like to see this board actively engaged in the making of railway rates, not simply putting their rubber stamp on the rates fixed by the railway corporations.

In surveys and inspections? We have three, I think, altogether.
And in the railways?

There is a great deal of
force in what the hon. member for Kingston has said. For years the government of this country has been over-staffed in regard to the survey and engineering forces. The minister stated that under an arrangement with the United States no tolls are charged on the canals. Would it not seem that Canada at the present time is keeping up more canals than the United States and that therefore it is a kind of one-sided bargain? Will that arrangement be

Supply-Railways and Canals
continued when the new Welland canal is completed? We will have probably $100,000,000 in the new Welland canal. Is that arrangement with the United States likely to be continued?

Unless some new arrangement is made, it will be continued. The tolls were removed from canals for the purpose of encouraging traffic through our own Canadian ports, and through our canals. It cannot be denied, I think, that every dollar you impose in tolls must come out of the produce or the cargo. There is no other way to pay it. The vessel owner will charge that much more in his expenses against the traffic that is being moved; eventually either the consignor or the consignee will pay it, and in those days it was thought wise, in the interests of the development of our country, that we should remove the tolls from the canal. My hon. friend is right. We have a greater investment in those canals, and Canadian vessels I think, outside of the canal at the Sault, do not use American canals to any great extent. But that is the arrangement between the two countries, and every year there has been no toll charged.
Does that apply to the Trent canal?
I think so.

When were the
tolls put on first? It appears to me when we had free trade between the two countries there was no toll and we had free use of the canal. Even after the Americans abolished free trade and put a restriction on Canadian goods we had free use of her canals. Was there any particular time when the tolls were put on on the canals?

I can remember when
there were tolls on the canals. I can go that far, but I cannot give my hon. friend any information as to the date. My deputy tells me they were taken off in 1898.
Mr. .COOTE: When the Canadian ambassador to Washington is appointed will the ambassador take up with the United States the matter of sharing the expense of these canals and bearing their fair share for expense of operation? I think Canada is paying far more than her share for the construction and upkeep of the canals between the international lakes, and I think it is a matter that might very well be taken up with the government at Washington. As to tolls: if tolls are charged on the canal, the amount would would have to be added to the cost of the goods, to be paid by the people whose goods 
were being transported. Is that not the place where the money should be collected, rather than from the taxpayers of the country? If this principle were to be adopted with regard to all our transportation, it seems to me it should naturally follow that we should build rights of way, keep them up, allow the railways to operate and charge sufficient to cover the cost of operation and keep the rolling stock in repair. Why should we furnish a free waterway for all these ships, to compete with our own railways, and make it so difficult for our railways to pay the cost of operation? We are furnishing the Trent canal free of tolls to the people who live in that neighbourhood, and certainly, if they are carrying any freight at all, they must come in competition with our railways. I think it is time this matter was carefully considered by the people of Canada. In western Canada we have no canals and no water transportation and the government is spending no money in providing anything of that sort. But they are providing facilities in some sections, and I think it is unfair to other sections of Canada where there is no water transportation. If the canals were made to pay interest on the cost of investment and the necessary upkeep of the staff on the canals, we might consider that we were getting a fair deal, but under the present arrangement I do not think we are. Has the minister any views to give the committee on that point?

I have not looked into
the arrangement itself or the negotiations which led up to it. There may be something in what my hon. friend says and there may be some other reason underlying it which I am not aware of at the present time. I think I may go this far, that when the ambassador starts for Washington I will call his attention to what my hon. friend says.

Would the hon. minister not go further with reference to this Trent canal, for instance, and the Rideau canal? Are there any tolls on the boats that convey freight up and down the canals? If not, is it not creating unfair competition against our national railways operating in those regions? For the life of me I cannot see why tolls should not be charged on the canal. We would not think of building a railway right of way and allowing the railway to come along and run trains over it and pay nothing. We even go so far as to keep up the canals and pay the men who operate the locks.

Is water competition not
a pretty good regulative rate?

pretty hard on the railways, and it is hard on the taxpayers. I find from the return before me that we have spent in Canada a grand total of $211,000,000 on canals. On what figures are those
percentages based? Percentages lead one astray unless one knows on what they are based.
On the freight rates that existed prior to 1916.
What were they?

Why is this St. Lawrence ship canal vote holding up the Morrisburg application of the Ontario government and the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission for

power which is so badly needed? I understand the government has taken the position that nothing will be done until this money is voted and a report made. It may be a year or two, or three or four or five years, before a report is made. In the meantime, the reports and the applications are all in, and I see no reason why the application of the Ontario Hydro Electric Commission and the Ontario government should not be granted. A joint report was made by the commission on this work from the financial side, the engineering side, the navigation side and the transportation side. It is a very good report. I cannot see what object will be gained by appointing a new commission. In addition to this, the appointment of this new commission is, holding up a very important power development for eastern Ontario. About a month ago the minister promised that when this vote was up, he would make a statement as to the Morris-burg proposition.

This item is larger than it was last year, but that is accounted for by the fact that heretofore we have been carrying an item of $50,000 in the estimates of the Railways and Canals department for this work, and now it is all put under the one head and made $150,000 instead of $100,000. My hon. friend has asked a question and it will take me a few minutes, perhaps, to explain the matter. As a matter of fact, the duty of this government is [primarily to look after the requirements of navigation. The question of an enlarged St. Lawrence waterway is viewed from three angles: First, those who want it developed for power purposes and have little interest in navigation; second, those who think altogether of navigation; and third, others who take into consideration both the development of power and the improvement of navigation. The federal authority must make navigation its primary care. Some years ago a joint board of engineers was appointed by the United States and Canada. That commission was composed of Mr. Wooten, representing the United States and the late Mr. Bowden, representing the Dominion of Canada, he being chief engineer of the Department of Railways and Canals.' This committee made a comprehensive study of the question and brought in a report. Without going into details, I may say that that report was favourable to this project.
In what year was that report made?

I think it was 1921, but I am not sure. The hon. member for North

Toronto (Mr. Church) asks: Why is this not proceeded with, after that report has been made? Let me point this out. Owing to the many questions that arise between Canada and the United States involving interests in water in streams, international and otherwise, the two governments arranged by treaty, some years ago, to name an international joint commission, to which is referred all questions concerning boundary waters. This question of the development of the St. Lawrence waterway was referred to the commission and the report of Messrs. Wooten and Bowden was submitted, if I remember rightly to it. While the engineers were studying the problem the International Joint Commission toured Canada and the United States, taking evidence as to the advisability of entering into an arrangement in regard to the St. Lawrence waterway, both countries being deeply interested. I appeared among others before the commission and gave what evidence I thought ought to be given. The International Joint Commission itself, after consideration of the report of the board of engineres decided that the scheme was practicable. It made a report recommending the project, but in that report the following significant paragraph appears:
The commission is convinced that in a matter of such unusual magnitude, involving engineering factors that are more or less debatable, and affecting the interests of many millions of people, too much care cannot be taken to ensure the adoption of plans that will be beyond reasonable criticism both as to the general scheme of development and the working out of its details. It is therefore desirable that before any steps are taken to carry out the commission's recommendation the plans of the engineering board, together with such comments or criticisms or alternative plans as have been filed with the commission by other engineers, should be referred back to the board and enlarged by other leading members of the engineering profession, to the end that the whole question be given that further and complete study that its magnitude and importance demand.
In view of that very positive recommendation the governments of both countries decided to proceed with a further investigation. There was a good deal of correspondence between the United States and Canada as to the questions which should be referred to the enlarged joint engineering board. That board included, in its Canadian section, D. W. McLachlan, of the Department of Railways and Canals, Oliver O. Lefehvre and Mitchell and Kelly and Pillsbury were appointed technical officers for the consideration of the term of reference which should constitute the instructions to the enlarged joint engineering board. One difficult question arose between the two countries and it required a good deal of correspondence to get it straightened out. Everyone understands or has some knowledge at least of the difficulties in connection with the diversion of water at Chicago, and while the actual diversion did not perhaps properly come within the scope of the investigation of the engineers, the Canadian government felt that the joint engineering board Should consider the effect which the lowering of the water through this diversion would have on the St. Lawrence project. The American government was of the opinion that the question of the diversion of water at Niagara Falls should also be considered by the engineers. The Canadian government took the view that the Niagara diversions did not affect the St. Lawrence scheme; we pointed out that the diversion of water there had no influence on the depth of the St. Lawrence or the works involved, for the simple reason that practically all the water used at Niagara returns to the Niagara river or into the waterways that flow into the St. Lawrence, while at Chicago the water which is diverted goes into the Mississippi watershed and is lost both to the Niagara and the St. Lawrence rivers. It Will be seen, from the terms of reference Which, with the consent of the committee I beg to place on Hansard, that the joint board of engineers will give consideration to the effect of the Chicago diversion on the St. Lawrence project and that the question of the division of water at Niagara is not involved:

The governments of Canada and the United States have accepted the recommendation, made by the International Joint Commission in its report dated 19th December, 1921, that the question of the development of the St. Lawrence river for navigation and for the supply of power be referred to an enlarged joint board of engineers.
It is desired that the new board should review the report dated 24th June, 1921, made by the late Mr. W. A. Bowden and Colonel W. P. Wooten, and that it should extend its enquiries to certain additional
matters with a view to supplying the technical information likely to be relevant to the proposals made in the report of the International Joint Commission above referred to. The new board is therefore charged at this time with reporting upon the following:
1.	Is the scheme for the improvement of the St. Lawrence waterway, presented by the board in its report of June 24th, 1921, practicable and does it provide to the best advantage, at this time and ultimately, for the development of the capacities and possibilities of the waterway?
2.	What alternative schemes, if any, would be better adapted to secure the ends desired, due consideration being given-
(a)	to any special international or local interests having an importance justifying exceptional consideration, and
(b)	to the extent and character of the damage through flooding and the probable effect of the works upon the formation of ice and the consequent effect on the flow of the river?
3.	Should the estimates of cost be revised and, if so, what are the revised estimates of cost having regard to alternative schemes?
4.	In order to assist either government to allocate the amounts chargeable to navigation and power, what would be the respective estimated costs for improving the river for navigation alone and for power alone?
5. To what extent may water levels in the St. Lawrence river at and below Montreal, as well as the river and lake levels generally, be affected by the execution of the project?
6.	(a) To what extent and in what manner are the natural water levels in the St. Lawrence river and on the lakes affected by diversions authorized by license by either Canada or the United States, from or in the St. Lawrence river watershed?
(b)	By what measures could the water levels or navigable depths affected by the diversions referred to in section 6 (a) be restored, and what would be the cost thereof?
(c) How much power could be developed on the St. Lawrence river with the water diverted from the watershed referred to in section 6 (a) under:
(1)	The plans recommended.
(2)	Alternative plans providing for a full practical development of the river.

To date the joint engineering board has had several meetings, and each section is also at work upon national aspects of the project.. Our national advisory committee has had two meetings. As to the development of power on the St. Lawrence, I think all Canada will agree with me it would be contrary to the recommendation of the International Joint Commission if any work for the development of power were proceeded with until this investigation

I have no particular objection to any of the men who have been named on any of these committees, but really I would not have thought anything quite so complicated was necessary. Under the late government we had a board, one single committee, which had arrived at very definite conclusions as to the general lines of the venture, as to where the dam should be, the nature of its construction and so on, and had compiled data which seemed very amply to support its view. I refer to the Dominion power board. Nominally it sat under my chairmanship, although I never was there; actually it was under the chairmanship of Mr. Challies, who now is on this interdepartmental committee. This is a question that the government has not attacked de novo at all. It has been under review departmentally for years. When the government came into office the Railway department had a most pronounced view on the subject. They had an engineer there by the name of Mr. Bowden, who is since deceased. Mr. Bowden was a member of the Dominion power board. He was most persevering in his own opinion. He never could be got to agree with the other members of the board; he had his plan which differed from the rest. Aside from that, however, there was no difference. Why we should have a committee of great political dignity and a galaxy of others, all filling the heavens at the same time, debating this matter year in and year out, I really do not know. I would not like to see any mistake made as to the development, but with the plans which the Dominion power board had worked out the Hydro-Electric Commission of Ontario were in accord, and the Hydro Electric Commission of Ontario, from the practical standpoint, with the experience they have behind them, would appear to me to be the body best entitled to speak as to how the whole thing should be managed. Of course I am aware that the responsibility of the Dominion is primarily from the standpoint of navigation. The navigation feature of this

enterprise is a big feature, but I do not think I could ever be persuaded that it is the major feature. The major feature is the power development, however we may cover it up under the lee of better navigation and so forth. Great advantage will come from better navigation of the St. Lawrence in the territory affected by the development, but it is comparatively meagre when compared with the commercial harvest that is expected to be reaped from the great potential power. I feel that the utmost consideration should be given to the views of the Hydro Electric Commission in this matter. They have undoubtedly made a success of the pioneering in power enterprises in this province. What they have done is to-day the outstanding example to the whole world of what can be achieved in the matter of great power development. I would be very sorry to see, in the first place, any plan adopted which is not in full harmony with the experience and matured opinions of that body, but I would be equally disappointed to find that by the interposition of a hopeless complex or endless devolution of machinery the aspirations of the people of Ontario for power from this enterprise are indefinitely postponed.

It is interesting to note how the system of the United States differs from ours in connection with this matter. Something has already been said in regard to engineering or survey services under an earlier item. I pointed out, or intended to point- out then that all these services should be really under one head. To-day the United States are dealing with this project under one department; the officers appointed by them to deal with it are permanent officials of their engineering services. Our system is so divided and subdivided that, like my leader, I have very little hope of a decision being arrived at in the matter. Certainly under the present methods it will take a great many years to reach anything dtefinite. The development of power i3 of very great importance to this country. Power can be developed on the St. Lawrence in a very few years, but the deepening of the St. Lawrence cannot be completed within from thirty to fifty years-I would say fifty, if we are to judge by the development of other projects now under way, the Welland canal for example. The country cannot afford to wait even thirty years for the development of this power. The Hydro Electric system had under consideration the question of the development of power on the St. Lawrence at two points. First they were willing to take power from a development at Waddington,
 <
N.Y., but that fell by the way. Then about 1912 or 1913 came the project of developing power at the Morrisburg dam. We have the assertion of the engineering department of the Hydro Electric system of Ontario that the development by means of this dam would not interfere with navigation on the St. Lawrence, but would rather improve it. I do not think we need hesitate to accept this view of the Hydro Electric engineering deportment, because they have already undertaken the development of power on the Chippewa river. That project is one of the greatest in North America, equal perhaps to anything in the world. I happened to be there about the time of its completion, when a survey of the work was being made by the greatest engineers of the American Department of Engineering. The men who had planned and brought to completion the great power development on the Mississippi river were there on that occasion, and they had no hesitation in saying that this was one of the most wonderful projects developed on this continent, or indeed on any continent. Consequently, I think we need not cast aside the opinion of a department like the Hydro Electric engineering department of Ontario, and they have already made the assertion that the development of power by the Morris-burg dam will not interfere with navigation on the St. Lawrence.
To shorten the matter, I would urge upon the minister that means be taken, to have a quick decision given as to the possibility of the development of power by the Morrisburg dam without interference with the other project. I do not see any reason why that decision should be delayed. The matter is urgent, and this power will be developed without any cost to the federal government or to this country. The matter should be brought to a head at once. Let the engineers who are now discussing it give their decision, and if their decision should be that it would interfere with the St. Lawrence project, we can sit quiet and say all right; we can afford to await a further opinion. But it is urgent that the engineers in connection with" this matter should not wait for the larger project, which of course, will be considered further, but should let us have a decision as to whether this Morrisburg development cannot be proceeded with at once.

I wish to commend the action of the government in one respect at least, that they are approaching this matter with caution. I do not know whether the method that is being followed is the best; I do not know whether the amount that is

being expended is too small or too large; but I am convinced that if this project is proceeded with at once it will be fatal to the best interests of Canada. Some years ago the Welland canal project was launched, and I think perhaps many would have taken at that time the same course the minister took. We were all optimistic, we had not got into the war, but now we can plainly see that the project was started too soon.
I would like to say a word on transportation in connection with the deepening of the St. Lawrence. I have little knowledge of the possibilities or of the necessity or the wisdom of proceeding to develop water-power, but the transportation side of this question is of interest to western Canada. Two years ago when we were discussing this matter, I pointed out that after the Welland canal was opened, great boats would be able to proceed to Prescott, and there the grain could be transferred and taken to Montreal, either by small boats or by rail, for a very few cents; in fact, I believe I said that even if the grain were transferred to elevators at Prescott and taken by rail, the cost in the large bulk would probably be only three or four cents; I am not sure as to the exact figure I stated. Now there is no good quoting a rate where there is no grain, or very little, moving. A few years ago the rate from Owen Sound and other points on the lakes, from transfer elevators to Montreal, was 5i cents; it is now, I believe, about 8 cents. It is quite plain to me that after the Welland canal is opened the cost of transferring grain at Prescott and taking it to Montreal is not going to be great. A small boat can take 80,000 bushels at a load, and which ever way it gcTes, the cost will be small. Double it again.

It might be. We can
plainly see that Canada is hardly in the financial position to stand this expenditure.
There is another reason why I think the government should approach this matter with great caution. When Mr. Hoover, who had been appointed chairman of the commission that has been referred to, came over into Canada, in about his very first speech he made the statement, if the newspapers quoted him correctly, that the commission was going
to report in favour of this project. I thought it would have been well for him to have first got the evidence and then have given his decision on the evidence, but rather it would seem he gave his decision first and was going to take the evidence after. There are many phases of this matter that require investigation. It is quite well known that the levels of the upper lakes are much lower than they were a few years ago. Possibly this project may lower the levels of the upper lakes still further. A loss of two or three feet, or even of one foot, when we consider the danger to navigation and the possibility of a big boat striking the bottom, is a very serious thing; it is difficult to estimate the loss there might be in that respect.
Looking back over the histoiy of our canals, we have had three Welland canals, and in each case the expectations of the traffic that was going to come through these canals were disappointed. electricity upon a fair basis of division, having regard to American rights to the water and also the Canadian rights.

The state of New York
has no more jurisdiction over it than the province of Ontario. The federal government of the United States and the federal government of Canada control navigation on the St. Lawrence.

I quite appreciate that; but he said that as far as the United States was concerned they needed the electricity and wanted it just as much as we did, and that if the navigation rights were absolutely secured-and that is the proposition-there would be no objection by the federal government. The hon. member for Welland (Mr. German) says that before you can put one foot of lumber into an international stream like the St. Lawrence, you have to get the consent of both federal governments. I am not arguing as to the right to power. That is a question for lawyers and I would not venture on that ground. The federal government have appointed representatives of Canada in the International Joint Com-

mission. That commission, having taken evidence all over Canada and the United States, having had the report of a joint engineering board composed of one man from Canada and one man from the United States, says to the people of both countries: Do not go on with this project until you have a further investigation by an enlarged engineering board. That is what we are doing. My view is that the United States-I do not speak positively, but I think I am correct-will not give their consent to any proposal affecting the international section of the St. Lawrence river until they have a report from the joint engineering board.

Is it not true that the construction of this dam at Mor-risburg would be in ease of future navigation work? To the extent that that dam iis put in, navigation is rendered more easy (When the complete scheme comes along.

It would be if the joint
engineering board should approve the Mor-risburg dam as part of the ultimate scheme. But they might report adversely to that feature, and say that that is not the best thing to do. I think it is fair to assume that neither government, on account of its obligations each to the other, could give its consent to the construction of a dam at Mor-risburg until the joint engineering body appointed by them to report on that scheme Lad made its report.

When is that
report expected?

I gave the date some
time ago. I think it is April, 1926, but my personal opinion is that it may be later, because anyone who has studied the question knows how involved the matter is.
I am afraid we shall have to look for reports and not for power.

I think my hon. friend
would do just as we are doing if he were charged with the responsibility. He would not delegate to his province or any other province the responsibility that belongs to the federal authority, and if he did, the province of Ontario could not deal with the United States; only the Dominion of Canada could deal with them.
Certainly.

Has the minister a report
including an estimate of the cost of the proposed international waterway?
$253,000,000, if I remember correctly the former engineer's report.

I take it from the remarks
made by the minister a few minutes ago that we can be assured the government do not contemplate engaging in any work in this connection until the report of this commission is received.

That is the position the
government must take.

I just wanted to be assured
of that, because, personally, with the limited information we have, I am very much opposed to this country entering upon the construction of the St. Lawrence waterway at the present time. We should first begin to pay off a little bit of the debt already incurred and finish other work which has been started.

Item agreed to.

Parliament voted $150,000 to aid in the construction of this bridge. We have paid $100,000 and this is to pay the balance of $50,000. The bridge was opened in June.

This money was voted by this parliament in order to aid a highway project which connects the province of Quebec with the province of Ontario and the west. The Ottawa river does not, in either of its branches, touch Ontario at this point, but a little west of that it is an interprovincial stream. The parliament of the time thought it was wise, in giving this aid to road construction, to aid in the construction of this bridge.

paid the balance.
