Item agreed to.
Trent canal-construction and betterments (revote, $17,000), $42,000.

Why should we spend more
money on capital account for the Trent canal?

This is for guard gates.
Severn division, payment for land damages, erection of lockmaster's house and some other small items. Hon. gentlemen will note, as I explained some time ago, there is not really a reduction in the item because the reduction was added to another place and taken from capital account here because we believed the items should be under another head.

We are spending $42,000 on
capital account. From what the minister says it seems to me that it should come under repair account. Why should the department carry items like these under capital account when they add nothing to our capital? Why not be honest and designate it properly?
If my hon. friend built himself a house would he not charge the cost to capital account?
But not if I built a new door on an old house.
These are not new doors; these are new constructions.
I do not know that it makes much difference; it is merely a matter of bookkeeping, because this is added to the net debt. We are not under the same illusion as in the case of the railways.
I think so, for the reason that this canal will not be worth fifty cents more after this expenditure is made than it is now.

Item agreed to.
Welland ship canal-construction, $15,000,000.

This is a large and important item and there is an increase of $4,000,000 as 308i
compared with last year, when we thought that the vote of $11,000,000 was quite large enough. I have had an opportunity of looking over the work on the Welland canal and I must say that when I saw it some time ago I was impressed with its magnitude. I studied to some extent the traffic passing through the canal and the estimate I got then has been corroborated to-day by the minister; that there was a traffic of some 5,000,000 tons over the canal last year. It struck me that the canal was giving very good service as it was, and at a time like this when our finances are more or less limited it did not seem to me advisable that the expenditures there should be increased. I discovered some time ago in answer to a question that the wofk on the Welland canal is expected to be completed in 1929. So far the expeditures on the canal total $51,203,488.15; that was up to the beginning of the present season. But as it is estimated that the total requirements for the work demand some $100,000,000, it will be seen that we have still something like $49,000,000 to provide before the canal will be completed. Spread that over five years, including the present year and the year 1929, and you have an annual expenditure of less than $10,000,000. Why therefore should we be spending $15,000,000 this year? That is what is bothering me. We have been spending rather lavishly too in other directions. For instance, there is an item of $5,000,000 for Quebec harbour. Is it necessary that we should spend $15,000,000 this year on -this work when other projects elsewhere are not, so far as we know, receiving very much consideration?
The Hudson Bay railway.

Yes, that is the very thing I had in mind. We may be told of course that as the session is not yet over there is still some prospect in that regard; but from all the information that is available, things do not look very promising. Under these circumstances I do not think I should be doing anything but what might be reasonably expected of me if I protested very strongly against so large a vote for the Welland canal. I move therefore that item 111 for the Welland ship canal construction be reduced by $5,000,000.

I do not think the hon. member can be serious. If he is, then, he has not the faintest idea of what a business proposition is. This work is all under contract except one section of it and if we refused to

Supply-Railways and Canals
carry out our contracts we should still have to pay the money, and that would be paying for work that is not done. Parliament cannot take any different position in business from that which any private person would assume. If my hon. friend had a man engaged to build a house for him he would want to have the work done as quickly as possible.
But I would try to provide the money before letting the contract.

The -money is always provided before the contracts are let. I repeat, this work is all under contract and we cannot afford not to carry it out. If the hon. member gave a man a contract to -build a house what would he do if somebody else came along and advised him not t-o put the roof on this year but to let the contractor discharge his workmen? Why, he would not think of such a thing for a moment either in his own interests -or as a matter of fair play to the contractor. The Welland canal was started at the request of the western people, and I say that emphatically because I know.
Did the minister ever receive -a request signed by 125,000 people of one province urging that this work be completed, as was done in the case of the Hudson Bay railway a few days ago?

The people of the west
urged the government to have this work done. I do not think my hon. friend was in the firing line then.
Yes, he was.

At any rate, they urged
the government to pledge itself to the completion of the Welland canal at the earliest possible date. That was the state of public opinion in that part of the country then, however it may have changed. I say emphatically that the WTelland canal was started largely at the request of the western people to reduce the cost of carrying their commodities. My hon. friend objects now and he gives as the reason for his objection the fact that the Hudson Bay railway is not getting a vote.
That is one of the reasons.

Well, that may be an excuse but it is no reason; it is not a reason that will carry my friend along. Suppose when the Hudson Bay railway started, members in parliament had refused to vote anything -for it because votes were not being asked for in connection with other undertakings. Would that have been any reason for not voting expenditures for that railway?

The point on which the
committee would like some information is whether it is absolutely necessary that the canal should be finished right away.

The longer it waits the
more it will cost. When the war came on the government of the day stopped construction and they had to settle with the contractors. After the war regular construction started again. I think hon. gentlemen have a wrong idea of the Welland canal, and I believe that no part of Canada would object more than the west, particularly those there who send their grain eastward, if we now stopped construction or retarded it. At the present rate it will take four years to finish the work. Does any hon. member think it would be good business to leave one section unconstructed? We -might as well stop work altogether, because the canal cannot be opened for use until every section is completed. Suppose we let up on the work, the canal could not be utilized and our investment would be idle.
Does the minister say it will take $15,000,000 annually for the next five years to complete the work?
I do not think it will.
A little more I think.

The contracts will be
completed as we go along, and as there is only one new contract to be let a less amount will be required each year. I think hon. gentlemen will see the wisdom of getting this work completed. I have not lost faith in the conviction I have expressed many times, that the completion of the Welland canal, so that grain can be carried in bulk down the St. Lawrence, will reduce the cost of carriage to a very marked extent.

The minister stated that
most of the requests for undertaking this work came from the western provinces. Was it from members of parliament, boards of trade, or the organized farmers' associations?

I think I am safe in saying that in one section of the west that Sir Wilfrid and I visited there was not one single point where we were not urged to start construction of the Welland canal. There was another body of people-a small body, but they have increased greatly in the meantime-[DOT] that urged the construction of the Hudson Bay railway. These were the two things urged on us throughout the whole trip. Of course, it is a matter of history now that the Pacific coast route has opened up. On my return

Supply-Railways and Canals
from that trip, even coming through the prairie provinces, I was laughed at for saying that in a few years they would be shipping some of their grain to the Pacific coast, because it was then objected that we could not ship grain through the tropics in bulk, it must be put in sacks, and so on. But as to the east bound traffic, I am still of the conviction that the men in the west who asked for the Welland ship canal were wise, and that we ought to complete it as soon as possible.

Was it mainly at the
request of western people that the government of the day started this project, or did not eastern representations have equal, if not more, weight with the administration? The minister says the contract was stopped when the war came on. That happened with the Hudson Bay route, too.
That was stopped afterwards, I think.

The government saw
their way clear to resume work on the Welland canal, but they forgot all about the Hudson Bay railway. I think they should treat both projects alike.

I am a little in doubt what course I should take towards the amendment. There is one aspect that I would point out. At the present time the cost of carrying grain from the head of the lakes down to Port Colbome runs from two and a quarter to four cents a bushel; that is for about a thousand miles. It costs about ten cents a bushel to carry that same grain a little over a third of that distance from Port Colborne to Montreal. There is a hundred and fifty miles of lake Ontario in the route that takes the higher rate, simply because the Welland canal will not permit of any more than light loading. With the completion of the Welland canal, that hundred and fifty miles of lake Ontario will belong to the route that takes the lower rate. For that reason I have felt a little more favourably inclined towards the Welland canal than perhaps have some of my colleagues because I believe it will be a greater benefit than some now realize; while I am convinced that the benefit from opening the St. Lawrence will be less than many anticipate. While I have no doubt whatever that the minister has ground for his statement that this canal was started largely because the west were asking for it, yet as against that I would say that although I was connected with farmers' organizations as far back as 1901, I never at any time heard any demand for this work; at least, I cannot remember any. However, the project has been started and a lot of money
invested in it, and unless it is completed a lot of the investment will stand idle.

The same with the
Hudson Bay railway.
True. I think both should be completed.

Mr. Chairman, I am
not at all convinced that the completion of the Welland canal will be any material factor in reducing grain rates on the lakes. One thing stands out clearly in the study of the situation, that the only real factor in keeping down the rates on traffic between the head of the lakes and Montreal is the competition from American sources. Grain is always carried at a cheaper rate on a mileage basis to the American ports than to our ports, and that again is determined almost entirely by the amount of coal and iron ore that is handled on the lakes. Anyone studying the situation will be struck with that fact. When the coal and iron ore traffic falls off, it leaves more shipping available for the handling of grain, and consequently the grain rates automatically go down; while during the period of active traffic in iron ore and coal those rates go up. One thing that has a great deal to do with this on the Canadian side is our coastal laws, Which prevent American ships bringing grain to Port Colborne, and is a great factor in diverting our grain to United States ports. After giving the matter a good deal of study, I am still to be convinced that this canal will ever he a factor in determining grain rates on the lakes.

Mr. Chairman, I am sure it
must be patent to all of us that if the Welland ship canal is to be of any real economic benefit to western Canada we must start to deepen the St. Lawrence river down to Montreal. I have stated on previous occasions that I do not believe the construction of the Welland ship canal will reduce the carrying Charges on grain one iota. The minister has accused us of not being sincere. Well, I do not think he is sincere when he tells this House-
Order.
Pardon me, I have never in my life accused a man in this House of being insincere; and I have never before been accused of insincerity myself.
Take it back.

I have been connected with
farmers' organizations in western Canada for over twenty years, and in all that time I never heard a demand for the Welland ship canal until I arrived in Ottawa. I am convinced that this project was commenced only at the instigation and on the request of the lake shipping companies. It is just like the deepening of our waterways-of the St. Lawrence, for example. We are deepening the St. Lawrence, spending some twenty to thirty millions before we get through, to satisfy an obsession on the part of the shipping companies who wish to build greater and greater boats. The same is true of the Welland ship canal. A number of us visited the Welland ship canal a few weeks ago and we were amazed at the extent of the project. The hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox) was well within the mark when he said that $50,000,000 more would be spent upon it. The engineer informed us that $60,000,000 would be required, and on the basis of former estimates in connection with the project, that will mean that the canal will cost us $130,000,000. I think the original estimate was $55,000,000. It has now reached $110,000,000 and will probably go to $125,000,000 or $130,000,000 before it is completed. The minister made some reference to contracts. Of course he was very careful not to mention the contract that was made with the western people for the completion of the Hudson Bay railway. There surely must have been a contract to complete that ninety-two miles of road where the grade was all built and the material was all on the ground for its completion. Eminent railway men have frequently stated that three months would have completed the road to the bay. In 1919 we had two debates on the Canadian Government Merchant Marine, for which this parliament voted $8,000,000, the excuse being given that the government must continue the merchant marine in order to give employment in and around Montreal. Sandwiched in between these two debates was the debate on the Hudson Bay railway, where the excuse given for the course adopted was lack of labour. At that time the deputy minister, whom we have with us to-day, stated that

$1,750,000 would complete the Hudson Bay railway, yet this parliament voted $8,000,000 for such a wild-cat scheme as the merchant marine. I wonder sometimes just what has happened in the last few years. What influences have been at work? I have before me a clipping from the Manitoba Free Press of 1890, which states:
The Manitoba members waited on Sir John Macdonald at Ottawa and presented a petition signed by 130 members of the House of Commons, asking the government to aid in construction of the Hudson Bay railway; Sir John promised to lay the question before his colleagues at the earliest possible date.
I have another clipping here from the Manitoba Free Press of 1895 which states that it was announced that the Dominion government would grant $2,500,000 for the Hudson Bay railway.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to
a point of order. We are not debating the Hudson Bay railway, and I do not think any member of the House should get up and make a statement such as the hon. member did without the Chair calling him to order.
I submit that the hon. member is perfectly in order, because he is only discussing the Hudson Bay railway by way of comparison.
You are doing that every day.

Was not the canal
started in 1823?

The Welland ship canal
was started in 1913.

They held a centennial
the other day.

It was started in 1913. We
had then been three years on our way with the Hudson Bay railway.

The hon. member for
Brantford (Mr. Raymond) is mistaken.
It started some time, anyway; what is the difference?

The minister again will refer to the matter of contracts. The Welland ship canal was only started at that time. A few survey parties were on the ground in 1913; some work was done in 1914 and 1915 and then work was suspended until 1919. At this date the Hudson Bay railway was practically completed. It has been questioned in this House whether the west has actually paid for the Hudson Bay railway.

I am simply proving my previous statement. My whole argument is based upon the minister's statement that the responsibility for the construction of the Welland canal is upon western Canada. That I contend is not correct.

Might I interject one word? I had the honour of going west with the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier in 1910, and I was present with him on several occasions when boards of trade and prominent business men in the west pressed on him the necessity of proceeding with the construction of the Welland canal.
Were there any representatives of the farmers' organizations in western Canada present?

In many
centres in the west representative public men
in their respective communities waited on Sir Wilfrid Laurier and asked for the construction of the Welland canal. I do not know who they were individually at this time.

I think the argument is
immaterial. We are also told in this House very frequently that railway charges in western Canada do not pay for the operation of the National railways, and that is given as an excuse why work should not be continued on the Hudson Bay railway.

I would like to know on
whose authority the hon. gentleman makes the statement that nobody in western Canada wanted the Welland canal. I think we did want it.

The press as a rule reflects
pretty well the sentiments of the people in any particular part of the country, and I defy any member of this House to show me one article in a newspaper in the last three years asking for the Welland canal.

Within the last two
years an association was formed in the city of Swift Current, called, I think, "The Greater Waterways Development Association," whose object it is to urge upon those in authority the necessity of proceeding with the development of this great waterways scheme.
I wonder what has become of that association. We have not heard anything of it for the last few years.
We get a circular from it every few days almost.

I have not heard the hon.
member for Maple Creek backing up that association very strongly.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to
a point of order, to ask that the hon. gentleman apologize for what he said to the right hon. Minister of Railways.

I think, Mr. Chairman, that
I have absolutely proved what I said at the outset.

Of course, for you said
nothing.

The newspapers tell us that
none of us say anything in this House. It is my intention to support the amendment of my hon. friend from Prince Albert (Mr. Knox). I think he has set forth certain reasons why we should not vote this large sum of money at this time. I do not believe Canada can afford a project such as the Welland ship canal, which we do not believe has any

Supply-Railways and Canals
economic value for the people of western Canada, who are charged with the responsibility for this project. It does 'look as though there might be some connection between this vote and the coming election. I am not sure whether that is so or not. I think, however, we are being very generous with the people of that part of Ontario, and with the shipping interests who will largely benefit by the construction of this canal, if we vote the sum of $10,000,000.

I had not intended to take any part in this debate, but on account of the extraordinary attitude taken by a very few western members I would like to say just a word. As one who lives in one of the great inland ports on the Great Lakes-
, Belle River?

The hon. gentleman should
not be so naughty. That expression is the pet remark Of the right hon. leader of the opposition. I should think the hon. gentleman himself in the course of two years might get an idea of his own. I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture is not here. I would like to draw his attention to a new western disease that apparently has arisen in a portion of Alberta. It seems to be grain on the brain. It ought to be stopped before it spreads any further into Ontario and the rest of the country.
Speaking for the city of Windsor, we are very anxious that the Welland canal work should be completed. Without ports such as we have at Windsor it would be very difficult to get revenue enough to run this country either now or in the future. I would just like to tell these gentlemen from the west that last year the direct revenue from the city of Windsor in customs and excise was twice as great from that one port alone, in the county of Essex, as the combined revenue from the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan. That only refers to customs and excise. If the direct revenue paid by the people who live in the port of Windsor and within a very few miles of it in income tax were compared, it would be found to be twice as the combined revenue of those two western provinces. We are willing in Ontario to cooperate with the west, and we have shown it in every way, but we do want a little cooperation from the west when we are trying to develop this great inland waterway. I would like to point this out to these few gentlemen who are objecting to everything we have in Ontario that seems to be making money for a district which seems to be progressing.
Do you not mean spending money?

If we are spending it, we are making double the amount for Canada as a whole. I have pointed1 out one very Strong argument in favour of the continuance of this work, and that applies to all the other inland ports, every one of them. I did] not believe a man lived in Canada, knowing anything about transportation, who was not absolutely convinced that the longer the water carriage which*lessens the rail haul the cheaper the rate even if you add only a hundred miles to the water transportation! and take it from the rail haul. We at Windsor load our canned goods on boats, tranship them at Montreal, send them around by the Panama canal, land them at Vancouver, and beat the rail rate from Windsor to Vancouver by 20 cents per case. Surely that is a demonstration of the argument that every mile added to the water carriage deducted . from the rail haul reduces your rate, and I would like a little co-operation from the west when we are trying to do some things in this part of Canada to build up our country.

I think the hon. member takes a rather peculiar way of asking for a little co-operation. He speaks of the amount collected in customs and excise taxes at the port of Windsor, and I wondered1 a bit, because that is the place, I think, at which the automobile parts are brought into this country which are later assembled into automobiles here, and sold to us at an advance of 37 per cent over the price in the United States, and in some cases at an increase of 41 per cent.
That is the same speech you made a month ago, and you were voted down.

My motion was voted down, and I did not get much co-operation from Ontario at that time. If there is one district in Canada that is receiving undue favours at the expense of the rest, it is the district surrounding Windsor, Ontario, where automobiles are manufactured.

The hon. member said that every mile added to the distance to foe travelled by water reduced the rate to be paid. Will he tell me how many miles a ship would have to go before the rate would be reduced to nothing?

The hon. member for North Essex made that statement and my hon. friend

should ask him that question. When, my hon. friend from North Essex was speaking about the amount of taxes they returned to the treasury there, I could not help but think that they must collect those taxes from somebody else. So far as automobiles are concerned they certainly do, and it reminded me of a certain class of people referred to in the New Testament, called the publicans. They were the tax collectors. They purchased from the government the privilege of collecting taxes from the people. They paid a certain amount to the Roman government and went out and collected all they could from the people. That is 'the position of certain people in the vicinity of Windsor. They are tax collectors for the Dominion of Canada, but they put so much in their own pockets through the process that they are liable for the biggest income tax of any part of the Dominion of Canada. If the hon. member for North Essex can find any glory for the people of Windsor out of this situation, let him have it.
To go back to the Welland ship canal, the item under discussion, we have already spent on this canal, we have been told, $51,000,000 odd. It is estimated by engineers that it will take another $60,000,000, making a total of $110,000,000, and if this estimate is no better than the estimates were in 1909 or 1910, it will run up to $125,000,000 or $150,000,000. But let us leave it at $110,000,000, and add to that the interest on the money put into this work every year and that will be put in every year until 1930, When the canal may be ready for operation, and you will find we will have an investment of $130,000,000 at least. The interest at five per cent would be $6,500,000, as we are paying at least five per cent on the money we are borrowing. That shows how much it will reduce the freight rate on grain! I find according to the statements given by the minister to-day that possibly 100 million bushels of grain came through the Welland canal last year. If you are going to spend $6,500,000 to reduce the carrying charges on 100 million bushels of grain, you are adopting an expensive method of reducing the freight rate. Before we would be justified in proceeding with the Welland ship canal, and before we are asked to vote on the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert, I think we should have some more information
from the Minister of Railways. We have not been given any reason why the construction requires so much more money this year than in previous years. We spent, in round figures, the following sums:

Last year we advanced to about $11,000,000. Why should we jump up this year to $15,000,000? I hope the minister will give us some explanation of that and tell us also what contracts are now entered into. This is information I asked for some weeks ago. I would like to know how many contracts there are, the amount necessary to complete them, new contracts are to be let, and what they are intended to cover, and what will be spent under them.

speechtext:
Before the
committee takes recess, I desire to lay upon the table two documents, one a note from the German government, February 9, 1925, and the other a note from the French government June 16, 1925, both relating to the German Security Pact proposal.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.
After Recess
The committee resumed at eight o'clock, Mr. Gordon in the chair.

When the committee rose at six o'clock, we were discussing the whole of the Welland canal. I suppose, Mr. Chairman, if you are adhering strictly to the rules, we would have to speak on the amendment alone, and in that case I would discuss only the amendment. But if you give the same latitude as other hon. members have had, I will take a few minutes to discuss the Welland canal. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) mentioned this afternoon that he thought all the members should visit the Welland canal and see it at close quarters. I was one of a party who visited the Welland canal this session; we went right from the lake Ontario end to the Port Colbome end, and as well we had a sail out on the lake around the harbour at Port Colbome.

Did the hon.
member see the Hydro-Electric too?

No, we did not. We did not see anything except the Welland canal. We

were not interested in anything except examining the locks and the wonderful digging and other work that was being carried on there. I would not say that Canada was wise in starting work on the Welland canal at the time she did, because, in my judgment, Canada should have had at least 20,000,000 of a population before commencing such a work as the Welland canal is. The unfortunate feature is that even after the work is completed-and it will not be completed until about 1930-no particular benefit will be derived from it, for this reason, that the boats which are now unloading at Port Col-iborne will simply be able to get through the ship canal and then they will have to unload at Prescott or Kingston. They will not be .able to get down to Montreal, and consequently no particular saving is to be effected by this work. I certainly would have been opposed to the work being started at the time it was, but in my opinion Canada cannot afford to stop the work to-day. It has gone on so far now that it cannot be stopped and it will have to be completed. There is such a quantity of plant, outfit and material on the ground that a tremendous loss of money fwould occur if the work were stopped, and a further tremendous amount of money would be required if the work were to be started up again. Although $15,000,000 which is going to be voted this year looks a huge sum, although it is going to take about that same amount of money every year until 1929 or 1930, and although it seems almost beyond reason to be voting such an amount of money, at the same time I hardly feel I can afford to support the amendment moved by the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Knox). I think the more money that is voted and spent wisely, the sooner that undertaking will be finished now that it has been started.

I wish to make a few remarks along the same lines as those of the hon. member for Macdonald (Mr. Lovie). Like the hon. member, I was one of a party who felt that we were discharging an obligation and, at the same time, fulfilling a very pleasant duty in inspecting the Welland canal. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) undertook to advise western members to inspect that great work. I venture to assert that more western members have visited that canal than, perhaps, members from Ontario and certainly members from Quebec or any of the other provinces. Emphasis has been laid upon the fact that this was started at the instance of the western people. I have no doubt that such was the case; but I think the minister knows, governments know, and mem-

Supply-Railways and Canals
bers of parliament know, that when persons interested want to get recommendations for a certain course of conduct, all they have to do is to circularize a certain number of people and they are sure to get those recommendations. I would suggest that possibly something of the same kind must have happened out in the west when pressure was brought to bear by various boards of trade on the government of the day to begin that work. I had the privilege of coming to Ottawa in 1910 with the farmers' delegation, and they made many demands upon the government, among them, of course, the Hudson Bay project, but I cannot recall that the Welland canal formed any part of the representations made to the government at that time. Certainly, during all my connection with the farmers' organization it has never been a subject of discussion. That, however, is not very much to the point at this juncture.
I had the pleasure of inspecting the Welland canal and, as a Canadian glad to see Canada doing big things in the world. I must say that it was a matter of pride to me to see the work that is being done there. No person who has not seen that work can form an adequate conception of the magnitude of it. I suppose, outside of the Panama canal, there are not many works that will exceed the Welland canal for magnitude and splendour when it is completed. At the same time, I have very grave doubts as to the wisdom of the undertaking in the first place. It might easily be demonstrated to-day that the interest on the money invested would have transported an immense quantity of grain from Georgian bay ports to Montreal by rail, and the present Welland canal would then have served all the other purposes for which a canal is required. One thing that was made clear to us the day we were there, was that the present canal is not large enough to accommodate the increasing traffic. We saw for ourselves that the traffic was becoming very congested. While there might be some criticism of the work as a commercial undertaking, there cannot be any criticism of it from the standpoint of a magnificent engineering feat. While it might be hard to prove that it is warranted as a commercial undertaking, now we are in it, like the hon. member for Macdonald I do not see how it can be stopped. Sometimes when you get into a bad place, the best thing to do is to make haste and get through as quickly as you can. As I view the matter at the present time, if this work is to be completed, as it certainly will be some time in the future, I do not see that anything can be gained by unnecessary
delay in the prosecution of it. A delay of one year would be of no value from the standpoint of economy. It would have to be five or ten years and by that time the plant that has already been installed would be in such a state of disrepair that a tremendous loss would be involved. I question very much the immediate effect of the Welland canal on grain rates; I do not think that the anticipations of those who so strongly advocate this project will be realized in the near future. At the same time I cannot see that there is anything else we can do than carry the work through to completion as speedily as possible.

If the present canal is
too small for the traffic that is going through it, what on earth is to be done but enlarge it?

I did not elaborate the
thought I had in mind. I can see that the interest on the amount that will be invested in the new canal would pay the freight from Georgian bay points to Montreal by rail on such a large quantity of wheat that the present canal would take care of all the other traffic. There is no question that the present canal will not accommodate all the traffic which will go on increasing in the next few years. With that situation in mind, and for the reasons I have already stated, I do not think it would be sound economy to delay the work unnecessarily. I do not feel that I could logically support the amendment. I do not know what commitments the government has made for the coming year, but in the absence of the fullest information I should not like to move that the item be cut down by any specified amount. Certainly I would not want to do that without a great deal more information than we have at the present time. In controversies of this kind we often get into illogical positions. The hon. member (Mr. Healy), who was properly attended to by the member for Macleod (Mr. Coote), made the mistake, which so many people make who come from eastern constituencies or from ports, of thinking that because these places are points of entry the people there are therefore paying all the duty. We have heard that argument from Montreal and Toronto and to-day we have had it from Windsor. Because it is a port of entry the people there are under the impression that all the duties collected at the port are by those in the immediate neighbourhood. As a matter of fact instead of their being taxpayers they are in a large measure tax collectors for the Dominion. It is such utterly absurd suggestions that sometimes lead us to question the

Supply-Railways and Canals
statements of hon. gentlemen on other subjects.

Since coming to the House
I have not heard anyone justify the expenditures on the Welland canal from the standpoint of freight traffic. After visiting the work that is going on there I have endeavoured to study canals generally to some extent. Although I do not pretend to have covered the entire field I must say that such literature as I have read on this subject does not incline me to justify the construction of the Welland ship canal. It seems to me that it is unwise to put these large expenditures into the project. I find two statements, one to the effect that it would reduce the cost of hauling wheat to the seaboard by 10 cents per bushel if the canal were completed. At present it costs less than 10 cents to carry wheat from Fort William to Montreal with the facilities we have, so that that statement is absurd. The other statement is that it would save the western farmers 5 cents a bushel. This is absurd too. As a matter of fact neither of these statements was signed; I do not know who the author was. Under the circumstances it is hardly to be wondered at that the western farmers, given to understand that they would be saved 10 cents a bushel on their freight, should clamour for the canal as suggested by the Minister of Railways.

Does my hon.
friend believe that it would save one cent a bushel if the big boats were enabled to go through?

If the hon. gentleman will
wait I shall come to that point. Now, this is the literature that has been circulated to justify the construction of the Welland ship canal and I claim that both of these statements are quite ridiculous. But apart from this, I have been looking into the subject generally and studying the history of canals. I find that the Welland ship canal is regarded as one of the outstanding feats of engineering, surpassed only by the Panama canal. Canals generally were at their best in the eighties but since that time the traffic has gone down rather than increased. I will admit that perhaps our canals are in a different class. I have been looking into the Manchester ship canal, connecting the city of Manchester, England, with the ocean. This canal has proved an absolute failure financially. To start with the engineers made the same mistake in connection with their estimates for the construction of the work as the average engineer does in this country, for the estimate was about half what the cost of construction proved to 
be on the completion of the work. People who were directly interested in it advocated the construction of the Manchester ship canal on the ground that ocean going vessels would be able to come right into the city of Manchester, but they found 'that the tonnage instead of increasing had diminished in the last few years. Ocean vessels rather than go up the thirty-five miles of canal unload at the seaboard, the freight being carried on by rail. The overhead in connection with the canal is so tremendous that the railways can compete,. and as a matter of fact they can cany the freight at a lower cost. The capital cost of the Manchester ship canal, which perhaps is nearest in comparison to the Welland canal, was $2,850,000 per mile while, if I am not mistaken, the Welland canal when completed will have a capital cost of about $5,000,000 per mile, or nearly twice as much. This being the case, I doubt very much that we shall ever be able to reduce the cost of transportation through the medium of this canal. We must remember too that the railway companies today are making great strides in the direction of cheaper transportation. They are able to load huge trains nowadays as compared with a few years ago and in this way they can carry freight at a lower rate. For that reason I do not believe that we shall effect very much of a reduction on the Welland canal. As I have said, I am not an authority on canals, but from the two or three books that I have read on the subject I have come to this conclusion. I understand that a few years ago the United States appointed a committee to investigate the canal situation in that country and also Europe, where there are a great many of these waterways, and the general report seemed to diiscourage further expenditures on construction so far as bringing about any reduction in transportation costs was concerned. Without going further, I am of the opinion from all the information that I have been able to gather on the subject, that there is very little chance of reducing the cost of transportation on the canals owing to the extremely high overhead. I should like to see the officials of the department prepare an estimate of the tonnage expected and the possible saving on freights by the use of the proposed canal. I may have been unforunale in reading authors not in favour of canals, but so far I have not seen one estimate substantiated, and I want to see something authentic as to the possible saving.

I was interested some time ago in reading some of the writings of Viscount Grey. All hon. members in this House, especially those to my right, will hold that gentleman in very high esteem. He certainly has never 'been characterized as in any degree revolutionary or radical. In his biography, which he has written in the form of memoirs, I find the following passages occur, and I wish to direct them to the attention of the Minister of National Defence and to this House, as much for the thought they express, as for the fact that they coincide very closely -indeed with the views I hold on this whole question of armaments-armaments alleged to be prepared for the purpose of defence. Viscount Grey has written this:
During the eleven years that I was Secretary of State for Foreign Affairs, every country had been piling up armaments and perfecting preparations for war. The object in each case had been security. The effect had been precisely the contrary to what was intended and desired.

Supply-Defence
Further on, having surveyed the general result of a policy of arming, that result being the stimulation of that sense of fear in the minds of nationals facing each other across a fortified boundary line, he says:
Such was the general condition of Europe as a result of this sense of fear. Preparations for war had produced fear, and fear predisposes to violence and catastrophe.	[DOT]
He then says:
The truer this comment is, the more force does it give to the conclusion that follows from it. If the allies, victors in the last war, pursue the same policy -viz; of arming-that Germany pursued after 1870 precisely the same untoward consequences will follow.
Those words certainly ought to strike those of us at least who are opposed to arming as a means of defence or as a means of security. In his conclusion, which is also contained in this article, Viscount Grey says:
Yet it should be possible for them, after the last war to find at least one common ground on which they (the nations of the world) could come together :n confident understanding; an agreement that in disputes between them war must be ruled out as a means of settlement; that between nations as between individuals the risk involved in settlement by law or arbitration is preferable to the disaster of force.
Again:
The future, the life of civilization, will depend upon whether a wiser and more instructive spirit prevails now than did before the last great war.
Now, Mr. Chairman, let us for a moment examine just what war is. Sherwood Eddy, a gentleman who prior to the entering of the United States into the conflict was an avowed militarist, wrote a book called "The Right to Fight," a most flaming criticism of the American attitude at that time, and in that book he did his best to drive all the best thought of America into an inflamed condition conducive to war. Now war itself taught him, as it taught those who went overseas, and as it ought to have taught those of us who were left, he was wrong. He has since that time become an avowed pacifist, and recently wrote a very splendid book, expressing views the contrary of those which he had written before. He avows bis own mistakes and he defines war as "an attempt to settle international disputes by armed military forces through organized destruction of life and property, in which each side seeks to impose its will upon the other by force. The end may be noble, motives exalted, but the end does not justify them. There are better ways."
I hold that view, Mr. Chairman. There are better ways. The Prime Minister recently gave voice to an utterance which appealed to me. I would hope that he would have brought to bear on a discussion so important as this
one, the great mind which was behind the thoughts which he at that time expressed. In the article to which I refer the Prime Minister said that these questions should be settled by reason, and he believed that we could settle international troubles by the use of reason, I believe so myself, but unfortunately we have never seriously attempted to apply reason to our international disputes.
On the other hand, you have the results of war itself. This gentleman, Mr. Sherwood Eddy, declares that the total cost of the last war, direct and indirect, in money value amounted to $337,000,000,000. He brings it nearer to our understanding by saying that the cost of the war would not yet be paid for if we had begun to pay on instalments of $20,000 per hour from the birth of Christ down to the present day. Twenty thousand dollars per hour! The war destroyed $9,000,000 worth an hour, or $215,000,000 worth a day. Yet, since the conflict is passed, we find all nations in the world employing chemists, employing scientists, employing the brains of human kind to develop more and fiercer implements of destruction.
Mr. Edison was recently asked if he believed the population of London could be killed by gas in twelve hours. He answered: "The thing could be done in three hours."
So impressed was Sir Eric Trithowen, of the British Air Force, by the tremendous power that could be exercised by air force in the event of another* conflict, that he stated recently he would, if he had the power, abolish the air as a means of attack. War is mass organized destruction of material wealth and property, and has left us a world with a millstone of debt about its neck, and with nothing accomplished of good for the human race.
I was interested some little time ago to ascertain just what benefits had accrued to civilization as a result of the last war, and in my studies I found some utterances of Mr. Clynes. In answer to Lord Birkenhead, at a meeting on the Geneva protocol, Mr. Clyne said this:
Look at a few of the great possessions that have come our way as the result of the sword. We have the greatest debt the world has ever known, and it is certain to last for generation after generation. The war has left us with thousands on thousands of acres of the most melancholy cemeteries the world has ever known, which have taken from us and from many other countries the flower of youth and manhood. That is what we have got from the war, debt and death, and the shaking of our moral standards in this and other countries. There is no cause to look to war for securing great possessions. War eats up and shatters possession. We, the greatest of the victors, have suffered loss of men, of money, of general status, and our peace of mind. The whole case against war is that it neither gets you anything nor settles anything.

Why should my hon. friend not apply those principles in peace-time. Why would he wait for a war in order to bring his principles into operation?
Unfortunately when a war comes along neither the Minister of Labour nor my hon. friend have any difficulty in finding ways to get round the British North America Act.
That is not an answer.
That is my answer. In time of peace, the aim, whether it be to secure old age pension or any other revenue, such as looking after the Cape Breton miners-
I am not asking about that. Why do you not advocate the application of those principles in peace-time?

I will be
glad to discuss that with my hon. friend when we discuss the question of capital levy.

If it is good in war time,
why should it not be good in peace time?

Let me
answer the question in this way. If the people who hold in their hands in this parliament the destiny of Canada continue to countenance and to hold up an economic system which is everlastingly beating down one great class and elevating a small minority into a place of power and wealth, then what the hon. member for Quebec South suggests will no doubt come to pass as a result of popular indignation.
That very system elevated my hon. friend to the position which he occupies to-day.
Remarks of that kind are after all quite excusable from the hon. member.
They are too true.

They are
certainly permissible from the hon. gentleman.
He is certainly here as a result of the system.
It is a very serious result, we shall admit.
That is my answer to the hon. member for Quebec South.
It is not too bad, but it is not a straight answer.

In time of war there should be demanded conscription of not only wealth, but every industry needed by the nation in such a period, and no industry should be allowed to grab off the huge profits in the way they were permitted to grab them off during the last war. Further, if this country would be willing to do it, I would gladly see it enter into an agreement or understanding with other nations to prevent the manufacture of arms by private individuals and the export of arms without the knowledge of the state. To-day, as a result of conflict, we have 'the people, not only of this country, but of all other countries engaged in the war and of many which were not, placing upon the backs of children yet unborn a debt which it will take them their lives to pay. Not only are those who are sitting here guilty of our participation in the past war and guilty for the manner in which we participated in ft, but they are guilty of placing upon the backs of still-to-be born children a debt which we ourselves are unable to meet. I ask that that condition of affairs be not continued, and instead of increasing the estimate for defence, the minister might look to reason rather than to force for the solution of these difficulties and, at least, reduce these estimates to the point at which they stood in the year 1913.

I want simply to make some general remarks, and they apply more particularly to the question of administration A number of questions have been placed upon the order paper with reference to a diminution of pay of members of the permanent force. I placed one on the order paper some time in April. I have not had an answer as yet; but I understand from outside sources that the pay and allowances of members of the perm-

Supply-Defence

anent force, with the exception always of members of the staff, have been reduced in the past year or two by twenty per cent. I wish to make my energetic protest against any discrimination in favour of the staff. If there is one portion of the militia estimates which should be diminished more than another, it is that which provides for payment of the staff and the fourteen, fifteen or sixteen generals whom we have in the Canadian army. If there is one portion of the militia estimates which should remain as it is, it is that which provides for payment of the underpaid noncommissioned officers, officers and junior officers of the permanent force. That the services of these men are useful to the country is being shown to-day when we have them down in the strike area. We must have some kind of a permanent force, and if we would have them, we must pay them some sort of salaries in order to get the best men to enter that force. At the present moment, our permanent force is top heavy. We are paying the higher officials far too much, and the junior officers, non-commissioned officers and men far too little. I am told that within the past two or three years there has been a substantial decrease in the salaries of those not on the staff and, in many cases, an increase in the salaries of those on the staff. For that reason I make my protest.
I have not in any way changed my views with reference to the annual training. Some years ago I stated in this House that the annual training, particularly of the country regiments, was expensive, useless and a burden on the country, and that it should be cut out altogether. With regard to expenses involved and undertaken by a certain number of militia officers for what some of my hon. friends have been pleased t'o call patriotic motives, may I say that while in a number of cases, perhaps, the motives of our colonels and honorary colonels are patriotic, in a large number of cases, in my humble judgment, the motives are derived purely from those of vanity and of wishing to place the title of colonel after their names and the red tab on their shoulders?
Is the title " colonel " not placed before the name?

It might be, but in all
probability other decorations will come after the name if they are colonels long enough.

wish in order to help recruiting to take their men on trips to United States points or different parts of this country, wish to clothe them in kilts when many of them never had the remotest right to being called Scotchmen, -if that right is anything to boast about,- wish to have them dressed in fine raiment and fancy feathers, let them pay for that. With regard to some remarks made by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr Woodsworth), I am usually in substantial agreement with him on questions relating to war and the horrors of war, and I do not yield to him in any respect in my detestation of everything that will go to encourage war or hate between nations. May I say first that this matter should never have been brought at this time to the attention of the public in any case, and though it may be distinctly contrary to order, I think it was none of the business of the British ministry to make public the information which they made public that twenty-five Canadian soldiers had been shot during the war and their invidious comparison when they stated that no Australian soldiers had been shot. As a matter of fact, no Australians were shot because the Australian government had expressly laid it down that none of their soldiers would be shot, no matter what crime they committed. Perhaps it would have been the duty of our government to make similar restrictions at that time; but the time is past and it is not for us now to decide on their conduct in that matter. But here were twenty-five men who left their wives and families or their relatives in this country. Are we at this stage, some ten years afterwards, to blazon in all the newspapers of Canada the crimes that they committed? Much as I admire the stand taken by my hon. friend from Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth),
I must say that what he is asking is simply that we bring a far greater calamity and far greater misery on the people of this country than they have already suffered.

I want to outline the
history of the cadet movement which was introduced in Canada by statute only as late as 1904. It was first thought of and talked of and formed by Sir Frederick Borden with the idea of building up a citizen soldiery. It authorizes the following things. First boys over twelve years of age who attend school may be formed into cadet corps; boys over fourteen and under eighteen may be formed into senior cadet corps; senior cadet corps or any portion thereof may be attached to any portion of the active militia for the purposes of drill and training. The principals of the schools may be instructors of cadets or the instructor may be any person having adequate qualifications. The qualifications of the instructor are gained free of charge, the expenses being paid by the state. The instructor in the school receives $2 per head for each cadet up to fifty and $1 per head for each cadet over that number.
I am opposed to cadet training in schools. I am opposed to it first because I believe that cadet training is not a good physical training. Experts in physical training bear me out in this, and I would quote briefly from Dudley A. Sargent of Harvard, physical instructor and medical doctor. He says:
Taking the most favourable view possible of military drill as a physical exercise, we are led to conclude that its strained positions and closely localised movements
309i
do not afford the essential requisites for developing the muscles and improving respiration and circulation, thereby improving the general health and condition of the system.
Let me now read from an extract taken from the Boston Medical and Surgical Journal.
This defect, we are pleased to state, is recognized by the great military nations of Europe, and measures are taken to give all the recruits from three to twelve months' gymnastic training to develop them as men, before they are expected to conform to the requiremenrs of the soldier.
Is not that exactly what is being done in our schools? All the training we give in the schools here is not confined to physical drill alone but it embraces as well gymnastic exercises.

I want to separate distinctly in the minds of the people physical exercise and military training. I believe in very much more physical education than we have to-day; it should be greatly increased. Indeed, the government would have to go a long way before they would hear me complain about the amount of money spent on physical education. I shall touch upon that point later. But military drill should not be confused in the public mind with physical training because the two are quite distinct things. Dr. Sargent goes on to say that if the people would account for the graceful poise of the cadets at West Point-he is referring to them particularly-they should visit that place in the summer and see the boys under the charge of a dancing master for one or two hours. There they have all forms of physical training and it is a splendid thing. It is not the military drill at all but the physical education which they get that is responsible for the erect carriage and the fine look of many of the cadets who spend four years in the military school. I quote once more from the director of physical training at the normal school at Pennsylvania:
That the military training as we know it now does not give the best physical training is evidenced by the fact that for years our military school at West Point and naval school at Annapolis have employed instructors of physical training to overcome the disastrous results of the one-sided practice of the manual of arms and other military drills.
Another reason against military training in schools is put so concisely by Dr. Sargent that I had better quote his words:
(5) Military drill in schools cannot teach boys the real art of war since they are too young to handle the rea. weapons and undergo the vigors of adequate instruction. Hence it is apt to foster a bombastic military spirit of tin-soldierism and a false sense of patriotism which does not appreciate the seriousness of war nor the glories of the struggles of peace.
Previous to the war a number of Toronto gentlemen, many of them reverend gentlemen,

as well as the inspector of schools there, prepared a pamphlet in favour of military training and it gives many reasons. It concludes with this strange reason:
That our system of government is democratic quadruples the force of arguments in favour of military dril. in schools; for the system tends to a disregard for authority, a due respect for which is restored by a reasonable system of universal military training.
That to me is an excellent reason why we should not have military training in schools. Are we afraid of democracy? One would think so when reading such reasons as this in support of military training in order to keep democracy in check. I want to quote again from a work on militarism written by an Englishman. This was at a time just following the war when there was a great wave of military enthusiasm, and when in England they tried to force compulsory military training at school, or cadet training. There was a great controversy on the subject, some taking one side and some the other.
Lord Methuen, writing to The Times advocating
compulsory military training, complacently remarked, "Wo worked on Lord Kitchener's admirable Australia scheme in forming the citizen army in South Africa. Little d'id we anticipate that within three years this force would have scotched a strike and quelled a rebellion.
Once more it would look to me as if cadet training is the real enemy of a democratic form of government. I challenge 'the right of the state to interfere in the education of the child. If we bring a child up to cherish a given ideal, and that ideal always remains the basis of its thought and action, and if by means of schools we repeat that process through all the people who form this or any other nation, we can quite plainly see that that ideal will determine the history of the nation for years. We might well ask ourselves in this young country: Is the child to be the central idea of education, or is the state? If education is for the benefit of the child, then we must think first of what is good for the child; if education is for the benefit of the state, then we must think of the state first, regardless of what it may do to the child. I want to quote Bernard Russell on this point. He too challenges the right of the state to influence or affect education. He says:
Education is a political weapon and could not exist if we respected the rights of children. If we respected the rights of children, we should educate them so as to give them the knowledge and the mental habits required for forming independent opinions; but education as a political institution endeavours to form habits and to circumscribe knowledge in such a way as to make one set of opinions inevitable.
That is what military training in schools does, and I want to point out to hon. mem-

bers that while we are not supposed to have compulsory military training in our secondary schools, that in reality and practice is what we have, and so the child's ideals and habits of thought along very many lines are circumscribed and are not what they might have been if the child were left to grow up unhampered by state interference.
Will my hon. friend explain what she means by saying that we have compulsory military training in the practical working out of our school system?

A boy who refuses to take military training is boycotted, he is discriminated against in sports by the teachers as well as by the pupils. I found that to be true in London, Ontario, and in many other places. I object to military training in schools as an educational feature-and it is supposed to be educational. We hear it said that military training in school makes for discipline. But we must not confuse external discipline with self-control. Self-control must be discipline of ourselves by ourselves; but discipline inflicted from without is not that same thing at all, and the tendency is rather for the children to go to greater extremes of indulgence, almost license, when the pressure of outside force is taken away.
I object to compulsory military training in schools because it confuses the regimental with the co-operative spirit. Boys are put in groups, it is quite true, but not in groups of their own choosing, not groups that gather around them spirits congenial to their own and that make for better mental and spiritual development of the boy, but enforced groups which usually have no social meaning. The president of the New York Evening Post says in regard to cadet training in schools: On moral grounds I believe the argument against :t is unanswerable. It falsifies values, lays emphasis on brute force, and makes directly against the ethical training which is supposed to be the teacher's first duty.
I oppose cadet training as a form of physical braining in schools-and that is what it is thought to mean-because by it girls are excluded from any sort of physical training. It is in reality more important to the future of the race that we should have women with good physique and healthy bodies than that we should have men with strong bodies. I believe that we should have a national system of physical education. If, whatever government is in power in the next parliament, should be willing to bring in a large vote under the Department of Health to set up a system of physical education, patterned possibly after the Swedish plan, I would wholeheartedly support it. After all, public opinion

makes governments do that which they languidly do, and I am confident that it would support such a move. I believe the people want physical training for children and youth, they want both boys and girls to have something that will give an outlet for their spirit of adventure. I think that this physical training could have all the lure of colour, of music, of form, that is now woven about military training in our schools. I believe that such a system would result in very much improving the health of our school children, and would leave Canada in a perfectly safe position, because if our future citizens have strong, well-developed bodies and unprejudiced and open minds, then Canada need not fear the future.
I have read quite a good deal on this subject, and I find that those who have made a life study of it claim that military training does not at all compete with sports in the developing of children, such traits as initiative, resourcefulness, co-operation, group loyalty. Games give very much greater chance for the developing of these desirable traits.
Possibly, though, the thing that we should most oppose this vote for is that by having military training in our schools the mind of the child is blinded, it is not led to think of any other means of settling international disputes other than this one method of war -this one method that has been absolutely discredited by all people who know most about it. Under this system the younger generation have no chance of having free ideals and shaping social evolution by their means, but instead they are shaped to the existing forms, to the idea of nationality which it pleases their rulers they should possess. I do not believe that was ever more true than it is to-day, although by this discussion and others that we have previously had in this House we have shown that there is an awakening in Canada, that there is another school of thought growing up in regard to military training. But it is too true that instead of letting the child think its way out, we superimpose upon it our false values, we put upon it what we, if we are honest with ourselves, have found to be unsound and unsafe, and we teach the child that that is the thing that will lead it to happiness in an international way.
Military training relies on force. It does not call out the highest or the best in humanity. It is pagan. I want to quote from a book entitled "West Point," by a man who just loves military training, so in whatever he says he will be perfectly fair about it. He is enthusiastic about military training, and in referring to the wonderful
chapel they have at West Point-he calls it an architect's dream-he says this:
The jewel of the interior is a great chancel window with its noble inscription:
"Erected to the glory of the God of Battles and .n faithful memory of the departed graduates of the United States Military Academy, West Point, by the living alumni".
Then he goes on to tell more about the beauty of it. He says:
There are twenty-seven panels each of which contains an almost life-size figure representing one of the chief militant figures of the Bible.
That is, they go back to pagan times to bring out ideals for the youth of to-day to worship.
Pagan ideals.

Yes, pagan ideals, and all the while we think of ourselves as Christian people, a people who have left pagan methods behind. It is true that in most things we have, but in this,one tremendous thing, this matter of adjusting international disputes, we are altogether pagan.
Who was the author my hon. friend just quoted?

Richardson. It is so easy to descend to brute force. In fact, sometimes I feel I have to work very hard to restrain myself from employing brute force, but still, one is always repaid for restraining. It is a much more difficult but a much greater thing to call upon the resources of mind and spirit than it is to bash one another's noses when we do not agree with each other's opinions, and that is what we have not learned to do internationally. Instead of bringing the best of our mind and the best of our spirit, the resources of ourselves, to bear on international questions, we simply descend to brute force. I do not care so much about the old men doing that; really I am not much concerned about it at all. But I am tremendously concerned that the old men before they pass on do not leave firmly imprinted on the mind of youth the impression that this is the highest and best way of settling things. There was a time when disputes between individuals were settled in that way-that is, when a man's honour was reflected upon-they had a duel, and whichever one was best won out and the other passed on. But now we do not have that, and people, I think, are quite as honourable as they used to be.
And quite as polite.

Yes, and quite as polite. Now, I notice that in Canada, if we find that other countries are doing a thing,

Possibly that last is one of the great lures, the class distinction offered by military training in schools, and the uniform and the music and the applause of watching crowds-all that appeals to children. When we go to school concerts at Christmas time, or to exercises at the commencement of the term, or to any place where children are performing, we know that they glory in interesting their elders, their relatives and friends. Until recently-it is almost true yet-the state, the school and the church condoned cadet training in schools- that is,^ they approved of it. Before these very buildings we have seen, when cadets were parading the silk hat of the politician, the robe of the divine, and the sober garb of the schoolmaster. I noticed that the schoolmasters trailed rather dismally a long piece behind the state and the church, but they got there just the same. So it is not surprising that the boys who are parading think it is a very fine thing when they can get the leaders of this country to come out and approve of and smile at what they are doing. And yet, pleasant as it looks on the beautiful green sward before these buildings-and despite the charm of colour, music, pomp, and class distinction-we must never forget that the spirit of the thing is the grinning demon of war. Amid all the beauty and all the music and all the colour, that is the dominant thing.

Empire Day! To my mind Empire Day has been degraded. I am ashamed of it. It is nothing but a flaunting of war in the face of people who would like to see the world live in peace. Why do they not show on Empire Day the things the empire is trying to do for civilzation, and the things that other netiorv' have done for civilization? Empire Day is made the occasion for nothing but a strutty, silly, pompous, bombastic performances by military men and those who are backing them. That as the training of young men for war is contrary to the spirit of Christ, it is resolved that we discontinue the officers' training corps in the schools of the United Church, and urge the government to abolish cadet training in the schools of the Dominion.
I think there is an ever-increasing body of people in Canada who are coming to the same conclusion, that military training in schools is bad for the boys. It is bad every way you think of it, mentally and phvsically. It is not an educational force, and should be entirely divorced from education. Among the bodies in Canada that have been protesting and are protesting against it is the
Parent-Teacher Federation of British Columbia-a most interesting thing. The Parent-Teacher Federation of British Columbia this year, helped, too by the Educational department of British Columbia-I almost think there must be some radicals living in British Columbia-put in a goodwill day, on the 18th of May, which was observed in nearly all the schools in British Columbia. It held up the ideal of trying to live at peace with the other nations of the world, rather than arming ourselves to some time attack them, or to protect ourselves against them.
The city of London last year held an interesting mass meeting at which all the bodies of that city were represented, a sort of community gathering of the city of London, and they protested against the whole business ot war and against this cadet training.
The United Farmers of Canada, through the Canadian Council of Agriculture, presented to the government, and I need not read it to them, a resolution asking that we cease this vote for cadet training in schools, that we cease cadet training in schools altogether, and substitute for it physical training that will have no connection with the military authorities at all.
The Trades and Labour Congress and the Trades Councils have for a great many years past been opposed to war, and particularly to this form of putting into our children's minds false ideals.
One could go on and on. There is no end to the material that is at hand. In fact, there is a whole literature to-day on this new school of thought that is coming up as against the old one of militarism, the new school of thought that is determined that the resources of the mind and the spirit will be given a chance to settle international discords. One might say from reading and talking to young people, after hearing the many things that are being said by young people, that a new spirit is emerging, and that that spirit is the spirit of youth. That youth is asking of its elders that they be allowed to find a way out, that they be allowed to think their way out unhampered by their elder's preconceived, and I might add, exploded ideas. If we had to go to the pacifists for proof that the last war amounted to very little now that it is all over, I would not expect hon. gentlemen in this chamber to listen to it, but when you can go to the people who had the most to do with the great war, and when they say the thing was a failure, that it got us out of nothing, that what caused the war still exists and, as Lloyd George says, exists in a greater degree than ever before, the causes

I think surely that is true.

I am sure
the House will agree with me that my hon. and gallant friend from Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) has delivered a very eloquent address, and the House will also agree with me, as I am sure every man and woman in the country will agree with me, that the last thing this country wants is war. Who wants war after the terrible catastrophe that overtook the whole world ten or eleven years ago? But war is not to be stopped by eloquent addresses such as that made by my hon. and gallant friend. War may occur from conditions over which neither she, nor any-else in this country, has any control whatever. I learned last year, when the opportunity came to me to visit the continent of Europe, about conditions existing there, under which war may arise at any time. It is conceded on all hands that the settlement and readjustment of the nations of Europe by the treaty of Versailles left conditions out of which difficulties may occur at any time. He said that reason was like a little sandbank in a wild and hungry ocean, but as the sandbank may increase gradually through the drifting of sand upon it, under the action of the storms and waves from all directions, so the accumulation of reason may grow in spite of the fury of the waves of passion and prejudice that beat upon it from all directions. I wish to recall to members of the House the outbreak of the Great war in 1914. At that time I, as I suppose most other Canadians, felt that although we experienced no great satisfaction in the outbreak of any war, we did feel that it was then practically unavoidable, and that we were bound in honour to go ahead with the enterprise when undertaken. I think too, as the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) has so well said, that most of the people in Canada and in all British countries had the highest motives in participating in that war, but I submit that the upshot of the war is very disturbing to the views then current. I should like to quote one expression which a newspaper friend of mine used at that time and which I think is very significant as embodying the conviction to which I feel myself driven by subsequent events. He was perhaps rather hot, and this is the way in which he put the whole matter:
Scoundrels at the top, fools at the bottom.
That was his summing up of the whole war. I must say that the more I have looked into the records, the more I am convinced that such is a fairly accurate description of that great catastrophe.
I think that is an insult- to our officers who went overseas and did splendid service, and I do not think it should be allowed to pass unchallenged in this House.
